title:
Hybrid Work Arrangement and Work-Life Balance of Women Employees
in Indian Public Sector Banks: A Secondary Data Analysis post pandemic

detail.title:
Hybrid Work Arrangement and Work-Life Balance of Women Employees
in Indian Public Sector Banks: A Secondary Data Analysis post pandemic
detail.abstract:
The increasing participation of women in India’s workforce has made it important to better understand how changing work patterns affect their work–life balance. According to official estimates, the female labour force participation rate has risen significantly in recent years, bringing greater attention to the working conditions of women employees. Within this broader context, women working in Indian public sector banks represent an important yet relatively underexplored group.

In the post-COVID period (2022–2025), hybrid work arrangements—where employees divide their time between office and remote work—have gradually emerged within the banking sector, though their adoption remains uneven. Despite this shift, limited research has examined how such arrangements influence the work–life balance of women employees in public sector banks.

This study is based on secondary data drawn from government reports, industry publications, corporate disclosures, and existing academic literature. Using Border Theory Sue Campbell Clark (2000) as a theoretical lens, work–life balance is examined through two dimensions: work interference with family (WIF) and family interference with work (FIW).

The analysis suggests that hybrid work offers certain benefits, particularly by reducing commuting time and allowing greater flexibility, which can ease work-related pressures on personal life. At the same time, it also creates challenges, as the overlap between home and work spaces can increase family-related interruptions during working hours. This mixed effect appears to be more pronounced for women with primary caregiving responsibilities.

The study concludes by highlighting both theoretical implications and practical considerations for human resource policies in public sector banks, while also suggesting directions for future research.

title: Electric Vehicle Fast-charging Facility Location with Endogenous Queuing in Path Selection
affiliations: , Institut de recherche d’Hydro-Qu´ebec, Varennes (Qc), Canada, HEC Montréal, HEC Montreal and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Electric Vehicle Fast-charging Facility Location with Endogenous Queuing in Path Selection
detail.abstract: As fast-charging demand grows, ensuring the operational resilience of electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure under congestion becomes a key challenge in large-scale transportation systems. We study a bilevel charging facility location problem in which EV drivers choose paths based on a disutility function incorporating travel time, charging stops, and queuing delays modeled via an M/M/c system. We develop both arc-flow and path-based bilevel formulations and derive equivalent single-level mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulations using strong duality and piecewise-linear approximations of queuing delays. To address the computational challenges arising from large-scale transportation networks, we propose an exact decomposition algorithm (DA) that iteratively solves a location master problem and an evaluation subproblem capturing path choice and congestion effects. Several acceleration strategies are introduced to improve convergence speed significantly. Computational results show that the proposed DA substantially outperforms the direct solution of the single-level MILP formulations using a commercial solver on small networks. Extensive experiments on large real-world networks from California and a case study in Quebec demonstrate strong scalability, with most instances solved to optimality or near-optimality within reasonable time limits. Benchmark comparisons on a closely related problem from the literature further show that the proposed DA consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithm in both solution quality and computational robustness.

title: Settlement Truncation in Impact Capital Markets: A Unified Theory of Delivery Failure

detail.title: Settlement Truncation in Impact Capital Markets: A Unified Theory of Delivery Failure
detail.abstract:
This paper establishes a rigorous theoretical framework explaining a persistent anomaly in impact capital markets: substantial volumes of committed capital consistently fail to translate into commensurate real-world delivery. Housing units remain unfinished; carbon credits expire unissued; health services go undelivered; approved loans await disbursement; enrolled participants never credential; and announced resilience funding remains unobligated. The conventional diagnoses—insufficient capital, misaligned incentives, or weak execution—systematically fail to identify the binding constraint.

The paper advances a structural explanation: in most impact domains, promised outcomes must transit an intermediary operator gate characterized by finite throughput capacity. These gates—permitting offices, verification bodies, compliance systems, underwriting pipelines, credentialing institutions, federal obligation processes—function as institutional chokepoints. When the volume of promised outcomes exceeds gate capacity, delivery becomes mechanically rationed regardless of available downstream capital.

detail.abstract: Sixty-five per cent of strategy investment is lost annually. Not because strategies are poorly conceived, but because the infrastructure to execute them has never been built (TRUE LOSS methodology, validated at 89.6% convergence against independent research; Arora 2026, SSRN 6488558). Yet the field lacks a unifying taxonomy explaining how this failure manifests. This paper synthesises 180+ academic, practitioner, and institutional sources, the product of 15 months of independent research spanning six decades of scholarship and approximately 2,500 years of strategies designed and executed by organisations, governments, and military institutions. To demonstrate the range and depth of this evidence base, ten sources are highlighted, from Nobel Prize-winning cognitive research (Kahneman and Tversky 1979) to the critical literature that challenged the field's own methodological foundations (Hughes 2011). The paper makes four contributions: (1) A five-pattern taxonomy identifying the universal mechanisms through which execution failure operates: Translation Loss, Coordination Friction, Adaptation Lag, Feedback Delay, and Commitment Decay. (2) A 14-barrier diagnostic model, classified into three severity tiers (Critical, Elevated, and Variable), mapping operational barriers to these five patterns across adoption and execution phases. (3) Cross-pattern interaction analysis demonstrating that approximately 70% of all possible pattern pairs exhibit measurable amplification or dampening effects, producing nearly 10,000 distinct diagnostic configurations calibrated across multiple client segments and regional contexts. (4) Convergence validation against Beer and Eisenstat's (2000) Six Silent Killers framework, confirming structural alignment and identifying a genuine extension in two dimensions that internally-focused frameworks do not address: external environmental change and strategic signal latency. The infrastructure gap in strategy execution is not a process failure. It is a missing category of organisational capability. The patterns are structural. The barriers are identifiable. The cost is 65% of all strategic investment.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into organizational decision processes, assisting in problem framing, option generation, and alternative evaluation prior to commitment. This development prompts critical questions for effectuation-a decision logic focused on action, commitment, and control under uncertainty-because effectuation traditionally assumes human-centered judgment, authority, and accountability. This study re-specifies effectuation for organizational contexts where GenAI contributes to decision construction. Employing a conceptual theory-adaptation approach, the analysis is situated at the organizational decision system level and investigates how GenAI alters the enactment of means, affordable loss, partnership, and control. The analysis also highlights two cross-cutting assumptions that become particularly salient with GenAI participation: cognitive effort allocation and accountability attribution. Decision boundaries are introduced as an organizational design construct that regulates admissibility, escalation, override, and accountability in joint human-GenAI decision contexts. A Decision-Boundary Process Framework is developed to distinguish augmented, hybrid, and delegated configurations, and to derive propositions linking these configurations to observable differences in means, affordable loss, partnership, control, evaluative effort, and accountability. The findings demonstrate that effectuation can be maintained under uncertainty when decision boundaries are intentionally designed.

title: Markup Centrality and International Incidence in Global Production Networks

detail.title: Markup Centrality and International Incidence in Global Production Networks
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework to measure how markups amplify prices through global production networks and to attribute final-demand price wedges to upstream country-industry sources. The approach defines a compound markup as the ratio of observed prices to counterfactual pure-cost prices that would prevail if all markups in the network were one. Using an inputoutput price model under a Cobb-Douglas benchmark, the method yields an implementable mapping from direct markups to network-propagated wedges and an exact decomposition into upstream contributions. The framework is implemented with the World Input-Output Database 2016 release. The decomposition identifies upstream nodes with high markup centrality and quantifies the international incidence of the aggregate wedge, including destination-specific attributions that separate domestic from foreign contributions. Compound markups provide a disciplined accounting of how market power propagates through global value chains, with most of the aggregate wedge explained by a small number of propagation rounds and concentrated upstream contributors.

title: Graham Employee Engagement Scale

detail.title: Graham Employee Engagement Scale
detail.abstract:
This employee engagement scale provides a holistic look about how employee engagement can be measured.
The level and presence or absence of engagement depend on the extent of the variables of corporeality (body), spatiality (space), relationality (relationships), and temporality (time).
The Graham Employee Engagement Scale showcases the four overarching elements that must be examined, i.e., body, time, space, and relations in determining the level of engagement and elements to be addressed in building engagement. Specifically, it is essential to consider everything about individuals and their environment to understand, predict, and change behavior such as engagement. The Graham Employee Engagement Scale is valuable for understanding, assessing, and developing employee engagement. The Graham Employee Engagement Scale helps to understand which facet of the lifeworlds to focus human resource interventions for developing and maintaining employees engagement.

title: Intraday Volatility Regimes via Unsupervised Machine Learning: Evidence from the NIFTY Index

detail.title: Intraday Volatility Regimes via Unsupervised Machine Learning: Evidence from the NIFTY Index
detail.abstract: We propose an unsupervised machine learning framework for identifying structured intraday volatility regimes in high-frequency financial data. Using 5-minute observations of the NIFTY index over the 2025 calendar year, we construct price-based features capturing realized volatility, volatility dynamics, and intrabar geometry. Nonlinear dimensionality reduction via Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is combined with density-based clustering using HDBSCAN to detect latent volatility states without imposing parametric distributional assumptions. The empirical analysis reveals a highly persistent baseline volatility regime punctuated by short-lived elevated volatility states. Estimated transition probabilities exhibit strong consistency with first-order Markov dynamics, and theoretical expected regime durations align closely with observed persistence patterns. Volatility-related features differ significantly across regimes, while return differences remain statistically insignificant, indicating that regime organization is primarily volatility-driven rather than drift-driven. Out-of-sample evaluation demonstrates that regime-conditioned forecasts reduce 30-minute realized volatility mean squared error by approximately 5.65% relative to a naive unconditional benchmark. These findings indicate that nonlinear unsupervised learning methods can uncover economically meaningful volatility structure and provide incremental short-horizon predictive value in high-frequency equity markets.

title: How Does the use of Forward Supply Contracts Influence Management Sales Forecasting?
affiliations: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: How Does the use of Forward Supply Contracts Influence Management Sales Forecasting?
detail.abstract: An important aspect of supply chain planning is the use of forward supply contracts (FSCs) to secure the future supply of production inputs. This study explores the relationship between FSCs and management sales forecasts (MSFs) using a unique dataset derived from textual analysis of SEC filings. Our findings indicate a positive association between FSCs and both the likelihood and frequency of MSFs by customer firms, consistent with FSCs safeguarding against suppliers' opportunistic increases in input prices when customer firms disclose information signaling strong product market demand. We find that the positive relationship between FSCs and MSFs is more pronounced when suppliers are more likely to exploit MSFs to raise input prices, such as when customer firms experience unexpectedly high product demand, have low bargaining power, or have low gross margins, and when suppliers face high inflation risk. Furthermore, the positive relationship becomes more pronounced when supplier trustworthiness is low. Our study presents novel empirical evidence that contracts designed to enhance supply chain planning promote the voluntary disclosure of forward-looking information via MSFs.

title: Dynamic Pricing under Data-Enabled Learning: When Do Platforms Offer Free Access?

detail.title: Dynamic Pricing under Data-Enabled Learning: When Do Platforms Offer Free Access?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Industrial Organization, Artificial Intelligence, Microeconomics

detail.abstract: This paper develops a two-period model of a monopolistic platform choosing among three pricing regimes: subscription (paid-only), freemium (free with limited quality), and open-access (free with full quality) under data-enabled learning. Second-period quality increases with first-period usage, creating a trade-off between immediate profit and data acquisition. Under across-user learning, freemium is optimal when the effort cost of usage is low and the learning scale is moderate. We then incorporate withinuser learning, whereby prior usage raises returning users' valuations in period 2. This strengthens the incentive to build an early user base, expanding the regions in which freemium and open-access are optimal. We further extend the model to incorporate advertising revenue and quality-dependent production costs, showing how these forces alter the relative profitability of the three regimes.

title: Optimizing Win-Win Strategies for Ecological Value and Economic Returns in Green Crowdfunding: Insights from Evolutionary Game Theory
affiliations: Macau University of Science and Technology and Jiaxing University

detail.title: Optimizing Win-Win Strategies for Ecological Value and Economic Returns in Green Crowdfunding: Insights from Evolutionary Game Theory
detail.abstract: Green crowdfunding has emerged in recent years as an important financing tool to support environmentally sustainable projects. However, compared to other crowdfunding projects, green crowdfunding still faces challenges in balancing the ecological value of projects with economic returns. This study develops an evolutionary game model to analyze strategic interactions in green crowdfunding, where initiators can choose between green and non-green projects, while investors decide to participate or not. By examining various profit structures and cost conditions, the model uncovers the dynamics of strategy diffusion and equilibrium states, identifying conditions under which green projects can achieve a stable “participate-green” equilibrium, fostering a win-win outcome. These insights broaden the application of evolutionary game theory in crowdfunding and offer practical guidance for platform designers and policymakers. The findings emphasize incentivizing green project profitability to encourage investor engagement, advancing sustainable financing strategies.

title: When Moral Identity Fails: The Structural Limits of Sustainable Consumption

detail.title: When Moral Identity Fails: The Structural Limits of Sustainable Consumption

detail.abstract: Sustainability research largely assumes that activating moral identity leads consumers to act accordingly. This research challenges that premise. Drawing on moral identity theory and scarcity perspective, we propose that moral activation increases identity salience, but its behavioural impact depends on execution conditions shaped by trade-offs and resource constraints. Across two studies, we test process linking moral activation to identity salience and subsequent behaviour across two product contexts (Household cleaner and detergent). Study 1 establishes the mechanism, showing that moral activation reliably enhances identity salience but does not consistently translate into behaviour. Study 2 employs multigroup structural equation modelling to examine whether the proposed mechanism holds under conditions of economic stratification. The findings reveal that the identity-behaviour relationship is unstable and contingent, varying across product contexts and economic conditions, and weakening or reversing when financial, functional, or habitual costs become salient. These results demonstrate that identity operates as a contingent, context-dependent mechanism rather than a stable driver of behaviour. By integrating identity-based explanation with resource constraints, this research reconceptualises sustainable consumption as a constraint-conditioned process in which consumers act not on who they are, but on what they can afford to be.

title: Empirical Validation of Cognitive-Derived Coding Constraints and Tokenization Asymmetries in LLM-Assisted Software Engineering

detail.title: Empirical Validation of Cognitive-Derived Coding Constraints and Tokenization Asymmetries in LLM-Assisted Software Engineering
detail.abstract: Two prior theoretical works in this series identified an unresolved tension in AI-assisted software engineering. Pereira (2026a) argued that naming conventions commonly adopted for human readability impose a hidden economic cost on LLM workflows through byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenization, but offered only analytical projections. Pereira (2026b) proposed that structural thresholds derived from cognitive science-the Cognitive-Derived Coding Constraints (CDCC)-should also define an efficiency frontier for LLM processing, a convergence hypothesis left without empirical support. This paper closes both gaps. We frame LLM output generation as an economic production function: given code artifacts as inputs, the LLM produces output tokens subject to a capacity constraint. We conduct three controlled experiments using a reproducible Python pipeline. Experiment 1 measures token count differentials across naming conventions for a corpus of 200 enterprise event identifiers.

title: Reintegrating the Syrian Financial Sector: A Framework for Economic Stabilisation, Governance, and Global Re-engagement

detail.title: Reintegrating the Syrian Financial Sector: A Framework for Economic Stabilisation, Governance, and Global Re-engagement
detail.abstract:
The fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 created a historic opening for Syria's economic reintegration, with the United States, United Kingdom, and European Union dismantling the sanctions architecture that had severed Syrian banks from the global financial system throughout the conflict. Yet sanctions removal alone has proven insufficient. Syria's banking sector remains practically isolated, trust in formal financial institutions has collapsed domestically, and international correspondent banks lack the compliance architecture needed to re-engage. With reconstruction costs estimated at $216 billion, the question is no longer what the law permits but what the system can actually deliver.

This paper argues that Syria's financial reintegration must be treated as a security imperative rather than a technical economic exercise. A transparent, regulated, and internationally connected banking sector is the mechanism through which reconstruction finance flows, illicit networks are displaced, and governance is operationalised. Without it, sanctions relief produces a permissive legal environment without a functioning financial one.

Drawing on precedents from Iraq's centralised compliance model and post-conflict frameworks applied in Rwanda and Sudan, the paper sets out eleven concrete recommendations across three dimensions: capacity building and compliance workforce development; supervisory reform and institutional development, including the restructuring of Syria's financial intelligence function to meet Egmont Group standards; and equitable access mechanisms to ensure SMEs and vulnerable communities benefit from reintegration. A phased implementation roadmap spanning 2026 to 2028 assigns clear responsibilities to Syrian authorities, international financial institutions, and private sector partners. The paper also proposes a vetted correspondent banking architecture and Humanitarian Exchange Facility to establish secure payment corridors for reconstruction finance ahead of full system rehabilitation.

title: From Impulse Buying to Product Returns in Live-Streaming Commerce: The Roles of Cognitive Dissonance and Preventive Service Recovery
affiliations: Suzhou Vocational University, Sichuan University and Yibin University

detail.title: From Impulse Buying to Product Returns in Live-Streaming Commerce: The Roles of Cognitive Dissonance and Preventive Service Recovery
detail.abstract: This study examines why impulse buying in live-streaming commerce leads to product return intention by integrating cognitive dissonance theory with service recovery research. Although prior studies have primarily focused on impulse buying as a driver of purchase conversion, less attention has been paid to its post-purchase consequences, particularly return behavior. Addressing this gap, this study proposes that product returns can be understood as a form of post-purchase psychological adjustment following impulsive decisions. Using survey data from 542 consumers with live-streaming shopping experience, the results show that impulse buying increases return intention through heightened cognitive dissonance. Preventive service recovery weakens the positive effect of impulse buying on cognitive dissonance, while environmental responsibility reduces the extent to which cognitive dissonance translates into return intention. This study contributes to e-commerce research by linking impulse buying to return behavior in live-streaming commerce and by identifying both managerial and consumer-level boundary conditions. It also provides practical implications for reducing excessive returns in digital retail environments.

title: Constitutional AI Governance in the Public Sector Precaution, Accountability, and the Limits of Automation

detail.title: Constitutional AI Governance in the Public Sector Precaution, Accountability, and the Limits of Automation

This paper draws on the author's professional experience in AI deployment and governance, including applied work in high-stakes domains such as compliance and public-sector-adjacent applications. The views expressed are the author's independent analysis and do not necessarily represent those of Starkdata.AI or any other organization. There are no other competing interests or financial relationships to disclose.

detail.abstract:
The deployment of artificial intelligence within public administration represents a structural transformation in the exercise of public power. Unlike private-sector applications, governmental uses of AI directly affect fundamental rights, legal obligations, and institutional legitimacy. As a result, the governance of public-sector AI cannot be treated solely as a technical or regulatory matter but must be understood as a constitutional issue.

This paper develops a framework for constitutional AI governance grounded in precaution, accountability, explainability, and human oversight. Drawing on the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act, the General Data Protection Regulation, principles of administrative law, and emerging practices from the AI Pact, it argues that public authorities function as operators of potentially high-risk regulated systems and therefore bear enhanced duties of justification, control, and supervision.

Using tax administration as a paradigmatic high-impact domain, the paper demonstrates that traditional compliance approaches designed for static information systems are inadequate for contemporary AI, whose risks emerge from dynamic interactions among models, data pipelines, institutional processes, and human behaviour. 

This paper advances a constitutional framework for AI governance in public administration, integrating EU regulatory requirements with administrative law principles to define conditions for legitimate algorithmic decision-making by the state.

It includes conservative risk classification, architectural embedding of governance mechanisms, strict data controls, prohibition of unsupervised autonomous learning in production, human fallback mechanisms, and explicit limits on automated decision-making with external legal effects.

The paper concludes that safe and legitimate use of AI in the public sector depends not primarily on technical safeguards, but on institutional design. 

Without a constitutional approach to AI governance, automation risks undermining due process, accountability, and public trust. 

Conversely, properly governed AI can enhance administrative capacity while preserving the rule of law.

title: Competence and Coherence: The Structural Foundations of Enterprise AI Readiness

detail.title: Competence and Coherence: The Structural Foundations of Enterprise AI Readiness
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess the competencies required for enterprise knowledge work: writing, analysis, reasoning, and the ability to operate tools programmatically. Knowledge work, however, requires more than competence. It requires context: knowledge of who, what, when, why, and in what state. Competence is a property of the model, context is a property of the enterprise's data architecture. This paper presents a formal decomposition of that architecture. We reduce enterprise operational data to a small set of ontological primitives, typed entities participating in defined state machines. We show how the enterprise software stack fragments this ontology across proprietary systems and demonstrate that human workers have historically served as an implicit integration layer bridging the resulting contextual gaps. Building on enterprise architecture research establishing that architectural choices constrain execution capability, we introduce a two-layer AI readiness framework: state readiness (is the current ontological state complete, coherent, legible, and operable?) and transition readiness (can the enterprise trace decisions through state mutations over time?). We identify coherence, the standardization of the enterprise's ontological representations, as the load-bearing dimension, and define AI readiness as a function of that coherence.

title: The Theater of Compliance: Why We Need Machine-Verifiable Proof

detail.title: The Theater of Compliance: Why We Need Machine-Verifiable Proof
detail.abstract: Traditional governance relies on "performative PDFs"-static documents that describe intent but fail at the point of execution. This paper argues for a paradigm shift toward machine-verifiable proof. By moving accountability from a lawyer's narrative to a technical artifact enforced at runtime (The Luevano Standard), organizations can bridge the gap between legal intent and algorithmic reality.

title: From Alignment to Judgment Why Reward-Based Safety Fails at AGI Scale and the Necessity of a Structural Governance Standard

detail.title: From Alignment to Judgment Why Reward-Based Safety Fails at AGI Scale and the Necessity of a Structural Governance Standard
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems approach the threshold of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), prevailing safety paradigms based on reward optimization, behavioral alignment, and post-hoc oversight reveal fundamental structural limitations. These mechanisms assume that system behavior can be controlled through incentives and empirical correction-an assumption that collapses under conditions of strategic autonomy, recursive selfoptimization, and long-horizon planning. This paper argues that AGI safety requires a structural transition: from alignment-based control to judgment-based governance. It introduces the necessity of embedding nonbypassable evaluative structures between cognition and action-structures that transform safety from a training objective into an immutable architectural property. The paper presents the O-L Architecture as a candidate reference framework for executable, auditable, and scalable AGI governance, suitable for adoption by regulatory bodies, standard-setting institutions, and multi-stakeholder consortia.

title: Design and Development of an AI-Based Habit Tracking and Motivational Feedback System

detail.title: Design and Development of an AI-Based Habit Tracking and Motivational Feedback System
detail.abstract: This project describes an AI-based Habit Tracking and Motivation System designed to help users build and sustain positive habits. The system enables users to register, create and manage habits, log daily activities, and monitor progress through an intuitive user interface featuring dashboards and visual reports. A robust backend and API layer handles habit operations, daily logging, and database management to ensure secure, scalable, and efficient data processing. The system incorporates an AI-driven motivational engine that delivers personalized feedback using rule-based logic, adaptive learning, and NLP-based templates, with optional support from external AI services. Advanced analytics and progress visualization modules analyze user behavior, recognize patterns, predict future outcomes, and provide improvement suggestions. Overall, the system combines intelligent automation, data-driven insights, and user-centered design to promote long-term habit formation and continuous self-improvement.

title: ScanIt: An AI and Blockchain Powered Open-Source Framework for Content Authenticity

detail.title: ScanIt: An AI and Blockchain Powered Open-Source Framework for Content Authenticity
detail.abstract:
The explosive growth of generative AI has triggered a trust crisis in digital media. High-stakes errors, such as Deloitte Australia's $290,000 refund caused by AI hallucinations [49] and the accidental publishing of prompt text by major newspapers [50], illustrate the scale of the problem. A major limitation of existing detection tools is their "black box" design; users are forced to trust a verdict without understanding the logic behind it, nor do these tools verify factual accuracy. This paper presents ScanIt, a fully open-source framework that integrates multimodel AI detection with retrieval-augmented source verification and blockchain storage. The AI layer identifies synthetic text through a weighted consensus of three distinct models, while the source tracer checks claims against live web indices to catch hallucinations. By establishing a tamper-proof chain of custody for every analysis report, ScanIt generates the "transparent digital evidence" needed to resolve disputes over authorship and due diligence.

title: Towards a University of Hybrid Intelligence

detail.title: Towards a University of Hybrid Intelligence
detail.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence into higher education represents a structural transformation in how knowledge is created and transmitted. This paper argues for a shift from a "replacement" mentality to an "enhancement" approach, where AI challenges and elevates unique human skills. Drawing on evidence from the OECD and UNESCO, it explores the "mirage of false mastery", where immediate performance gains can mask the erosion of deep learning and critical thinking. To mitigate these risks, the paper advocates for a "Slow AI" strategy-using AI as a Socratic partner to refine creative thinking rather than an oracle for quick answers. Furthermore, it emphasizes the necessity of developing "hybrid human-AI skills" to address the digital skills gap, where only 56% of Europeans currently possess basic digital literacy. The conclusion proposes a move toward "pedagogical sovereignty" through specialized "EdGPT" models and "Teacher-AI Teaming" to ensure that universities foster critical hybrid intelligence rather than passive technological execution.

title: Optimizing Win-Win Strategies for Ecological Value and Economic Returns in Green Crowdfunding: Insights from Evolutionary Game Theory

detail.title: Optimizing Win-Win Strategies for Ecological Value and Economic Returns in Green Crowdfunding: Insights from Evolutionary Game Theory
detail.abstract: Green crowdfunding has emerged in recent years as an important financing tool to support environmentally sustainable projects. However, compared to other crowdfunding projects, green crowdfunding still faces challenges in balancing the ecological value of projects with economic returns. This study develops an evolutionary game model to analyze strategic interactions in green crowdfunding, where initiators can choose between green and non-green projects, while investors decide to participate or not. By examining various profit structures and cost conditions, the model uncovers the dynamics of strategy diffusion and equilibrium states, identifying conditions under which green projects can achieve a stable “participate-green” equilibrium, fostering a win-win outcome. These insights broaden the application of evolutionary game theory in crowdfunding and offer practical guidance for platform designers and policymakers. The findings emphasize incentivizing green project profitability to encourage investor engagement, advancing sustainable financing strategies.

title: The Economics and Financing of ASEAN Power Grid

detail.title: The Economics and Financing of ASEAN Power Grid

detail.abstract: This article examines the economic and strategic case for accelerating the ASEAN Power Grid (APG) as a foundation for regional energy security, decarbonization, and market integration. It argues that while ASEAN countries have advanced renewable energy targets and bilateral interconnections, the region remains fragmented by weak cross-border market architecture, inconsistent wheeling charges, and limited regulatory harmonization. Drawing on global examples of regional power pools, the article highlights how standardized transmission pricing, transparent settlement systems, and coordinated regulatory frameworks can unlock cross-border electricity trade and reduce system-wide costs. It evaluates the financing challenges of new interconnectors, the role of multilateral development banks, and the need for risk-sharing mechanisms to crowd in private capital. The central claim is that the ASEAN Power Grid is not merely an infrastructure project but an institutional reform agenda—one that can strengthen energy resilience, deepen regional integration, and enhance ASEAN’s global relevance in the clean energy transition.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the barriers and drivers of digitalization in small-and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Specifically, the study aimed to identify the key factors influencing the adoption and implementation of digital technologies in SMEs, understand the challenges faced by these organizations in their digital transformation journey. In this study, a fuzzy logic methodology was employed to assess the digitalization process of 4531 SMEs. Additionally, an analytical hierarchy process (AHP) was applied to determine the weights of the dimensions in the fuzzy analysis. This allowed for a more accurate and precise assessment of the digitalization levels in SMEs. The study revealed that insufficient financial resources, high investment costs, resistance from workers, a shortage of well-qualified staff, lack of knowledge about technology providers, high IT security requirements, the absence of a digital transformation-oriented business culture, and the application of fuzzy logic as a methodology were the key findings in the digitalization process of SMEs. title: Safety Under Scarcity in South Africa: A Perception-Based Analysis of Institutional Choice in a Vignette Survey Study

detail.title: Safety Under Scarcity in South Africa: A Perception-Based Analysis of Institutional Choice in a Vignette Survey Study
detail.abstract:
Financial scarcity shapes decision-making not only by constraining resources but also by altering how institutions are perceived. This study examines how subjective stress associated with financial scarcity relates to perceptions of institutional safety, trust, comprehension, and control, and how these perceptions influence preferences for formal and informal financial systems in South Africa. A web-based survey (N = 404) incorporating a standardised scarcity vignette, multidimensional perception ratings, and a behavioural choice task is used to evaluate a perception-based scarcity pathway.

Results indicate that scarcity-related stress is strongly associated with shifts in institutional perceptions, accounting for approximately 17% - 26% of the variance in composite safety evaluations across banks, stokvels, and mashonisas. Logistic regression and mediation analyses demonstrate that perceived bank safety statistically mediates nearly the entire association between stress and institutional choice, while the direct effect of stress on choice is negligible. Contrary to some scarcity models that predict institutional avoidance under financial strain, higher stress in this context is associated with slightly increased perceived bank safety and a modest reduction in informal system choice.

These findings refine behavioural scarcity theory by emphasising perceptual and relational mechanisms as the principal link between stress and financial behaviour. Financial decision-making under constraint appears to operate primarily through evaluations of institutional safety rather than through stress alone, with implications for financial inclusion policy and the maintenance of institutional trust.

title: Passive Investing, Diversification Risk and Financial Stability

detail.title: Passive Investing, Diversification Risk and Financial Stability
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the rise of passive investing affects the equity market's capacity to distribute aggregate risk. Using a valuation-adjusted Bartik instrument, I establish that a one-standard-deviation increase in passive ownership raises average pairwise stock return correlations by 9 percentage points. Through a structural demand-system framework, I decompose portfolio risk into correlation and idiosyncraticvolatility components and uncover two opposing forces: passive investing synchronizes asset returns through common, price-insensitive demand shocks, while simultaneously dampening firm-specific volatility. The correlation effect dominates. Relative to a counterfactual economy without passive investors, diversification benefits in the global minimum variance portfolio are 3% lower and its minimum achievable volatility is 19% higher; for the risk parity portfolio the losses are larger, at 9.5% and 25% respectively. Welfare costs concentrate among large, well-diversified institutions and are amplified during recessions-precisely when effective diversification matters most.

title: Financial Relativity: An Information-Geometric Interpretation of Asset Pricing
affiliations: East China University of Science and Technology (ECUST)

detail.title: Financial Relativity: An Information-Geometric Interpretation of Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Classical asset pricing relies on the risk-neutral measure Q for valuation, yet its economic meaning is typically grounded in a physical measure P. This creates an implicit asymmetry: pricing is governed by Q, while interpretation is anchored in P. As a result, the same pricing relation may admit multiple, and sometimes conflicting, explanations depending on how the link between P and Q is specified, making it difficult to provide a unified account of asset pricing within a single conceptual framework. This paper proposes an alternative perspective based on information geometry, termed financial relativity. The central principle is a relativity of probabilistic reference frames: P and Q possess no intrinsic hierarchy, but instead correspond to geometric structures induced by different informational constraints. Terminal structural information determines how probability geometry is shaped, and this geometry in turn governs how information is expressed in prices. Within this framework, the risk-neutral measure is reinterpreted as a posterior probability geometry shaped by structural constraints. Asset prices are characterized as geometric projections of terminal payoffs onto information subspaces, and price dynamics emerge as the progressive manifestation of structural information under evolving geometry. We develop discrete and continuous financial field equations to describe the formation of probability geometry, and derive geodesic price dynamics in which volatility is endogenously determined by posterior uncertainty. This framework provides a unified explanation for price fluctuations, event-driven dynamics, and risk premia, and yields testable implications, including structural links between volatility and posterior variance, as well as measures of the informational efficiency of prices. By integrating structural information, probability measures, and price dynamics within a unified geometric framework, the paper offers a coherent, extensible, and empirically tractable reinterpretation of asset pricing theory.

detail.abstract: This article argues for the removal of the 12% value-added tax (VAT) on electricity in the Philippines as an immediate response to the cost-of-living crisis and declining public trust in government. While technocratic objections focus on the estimated revenue loss of roughly ₱110 billion annually and concerns about tax efficiency and regressivity, the article contends that these assessments ignore broader economic dynamics. Removing VAT would restore purchasing power to households and firms, generate multiplier effects, ease cost-push inflation, and improve competitiveness in an already high-cost power environment. The policy can be designed progressively through lifeline consumption thresholds and time-bound triggers to safeguard fiscal stability. Beyond economics, the reform addresses tax morale and public trust by signaling fairness during a period of visible corruption and hardship. The central claim is that VAT removal is both sound short-term economics and necessary political economy reform.

detail.abstract: Ambitious climate targets are defined in Germany to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 65% by 2030 and reach to climate-neutrality by 2045. To facilitate this goal, by the early 2020s, the European Union and Germany have introduced significant support schemes through various regulatory frameworks. Although new regulatory frameworks aim to intensify and expedite efforts to reach to the targets, they have led to conflicts and inconsistencies considering sector-specific characteristics of each regulatory domain. Thus, the concept of policy coherence has become a critical aspect, specifically in cross-sectoral landscapes, where the implementation of low-emission technologies or fuels are affected by different regulatory domains. Power-to-X (PtX) fuels can be considered as an important example in this regard. The regulatory landscape governing PtX fuels is highly complex and covers several sectors, which have led to overlapping mandates, conflicting instruments and goals, and institutional fragmentation. Therefore, to understand the regulatory dynamics influencing the development of PtX fuels, it is significant to understand how policies interact, whether they support, contradict, or exhibit mixed trade-offs with one another. Additionally, in this cross-sectoral landscape, it is important to not only assess formal policy linkages but also to understand how coherence is perceived by experts and stakeholders. To address this challenge, we employ a mixed-method analytical approach for assessing perceived policy coherence of PtX fuels in Germany. Our approach builds on earlier qualitative studies by adding systematic and quantitative measures. Network analysis, Shannon's entropy, and principal component analysis are used to enable a structured understanding of policy interactions, distribution of influence, and coherence patterns.

detail.abstract: This study analyze the behavior and trend of the Effective Tax Rate (ETR) of selected Nifty 50 companies over a multi-year period. The Effective Tax Rate is calculated as the ratio of cash taxes paid to profit before tax, which provides a more realistic measure of the actual tax burden faced by a company. The analysis is based on firm-level financial data collected from Screener.in, where standardized multi-year financial statement data of publicly listed companies is available. The findings show that there is significant variation in ETR across firms and sectors. This variation is mainly driven by differences in profitability, sector-specific tax incentives, and accounting adjustments. In some cases, extremely high or negative ETR values were observed, largely due to the denominator effect arising from low or negative profit before tax rather than any structural change in the company's actual tax burden. Despite this volatility, the later years of the sample period indicate a gradual decline and stabilization in the Effective Tax Rate, suggesting better alignment with the statutory corporate tax framework. The sectoral analysis further reveals that cyclical industries tend to experience higher ETR volatility, whereas stable sectors exhibit more predictable and smoother tax incidence. Overall, this study provides useful insights for investors, policymakers, and researchers, as it helps in understanding the dynamics of corporate tax burden and highlights its implications for earnings predictability and firm valuation.

title: Stablecoin Fragility in a Segmented Open Economy

detail.title: Stablecoin Fragility in a Segmented Open Economy
detail.abstract: Stablecoins, privately issued digital dollar proxies, are widely viewed as accessible safe-haven substitutes for the U.S. dollar. This paper examines whether they inherit the safe-haven properties of their underlying fiat anchor during localized crises. Exploiting the December 3, 2024 South Korean martial law declaration as a quasi-natural experiment, we show that USD-backed stablecoins failed to appreciate alongside the onshore KRW/USD exchange rate and instead traded at a significant discount relative to parity. The depreciation was substantially larger for USDT than for USDC, driven by differences in funding pressure across stablecoins. A parsimonious framework links this heterogeneous depreciation to market segmentation and funding pressures. Our findings suggest that in segmented small open economies, privately issued digital dollar proxies may fail to function as safe-haven during stress episodes, decoupling from their fiat anchor precisely when the hedge is needed most.

detail.abstract: This study examines how the diffusion of heated tobacco products (HTPs) has affected cigarette consumption, smoking prevalence, and tobacco tax revenues in Japan. Using annual data for 1985-2024, we estimate long-run and error-correction interrupted time-series models incorporating taxation, income, secular trends, and structural changes associated with the introduction of HTPs in 2016. The results indicate that while cigarette taxation contributes to the long-run decline in smoking, HTP diffusion is associated with a larger reduction in cigarette consumption than can be explained by tax changes alone, with a more gradual decline in prevalence. Projection simulations suggest that continued HTP diffusion could bring cigarette prevalence close to commonly used smoke-free levels within the next two decades. At the same time, substitution from cigarettes to HTPs helps stabilize tobacco excise revenues by offsetting declining cigarette tax receipts. These findings suggest that in mature tobacco markets, the transition toward low smoking prevalence may increasingly occur through product substitution rather than taxation alone, with important implications for tobacco control policy and fiscal planning.

detail.abstract:
Delaware Senate Bill 21 (“SB 21”) has been widely framed as a politically motivated response to corporate flight, billionaire backlash, and perceived judicial overreach in controlling-shareholder doctrine. This Article argues that those accounts miss one of SB 21’s most consequential legal developments: its redefinition of the boundary between shareholder influence and corporate control. By replacing Delaware’s open-ended “actual control” doctrine with a statutory framework anchored in ownership thresholds and board-level authority, SB 21 transforms control from an ex post judicial determination into an ex-ante design choice.
Through doctrinal analysis and original qualitative interviews with leading corporate advisors, this Article shows how SB 21 stabilizes transaction planning while formally insulating traditional forms of minority shareholder engagement—persuasion, voting, proxy contests, and limited board representation—from fiduciary status below a one-third ownership threshold. The statute’s effects extend well beyond founder-led firms, reshaping the governance strategies of private equity sponsors, venture capital funds, and activist investors. Finally, this Article underscores how SB 21 simultaneously blesses increasingly aggressive minority-stake engagement while leaving unresolved—and in some cases exacerbating—new forms of contractual and economic control. Ultimately, SB 21 does not merely respond to recent cases; it recasts the law of corporate control itself, with lasting consequences for shareholder activism, private ordering, and the future of fiduciary accountability in Delaware corporate law.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether localised commuting-time advantages are reflected in residential property prices in a polycentric urban setting. Using Budapest as a case study, we combine multimodal origin-destination commuting data from the city's transport model with spatially detailed housing price data to assess the extent to which the commuting-housing trade-off remains relevant beyond the obvious monocentric structure. We estimate non-parametric distance gradients for average commuting times and housing prices relative to the CBD, and then compare the spatial pattern of model residuals to identify deviations from monocentricity. The results show that strong monocentric gradients persist in both variables, while also highlighting several outer and intermediate zones with better-thanexpected commuting accessibility. These accessibility advantages are only partly reflected in housing prices, suggesting that transport-related benefits are not fully capitalised into the residential market. The findings indicate that commuting accessibility remains an important organising force in urban space, but that its effects on residential prices are mediated by broader neighbourhood characteristics and housing market conditions.

title: A Tutorial on Cognitive Optimization in External Memory Systems: Reinterpreting Stolfi's Layers and Currier's Partitions as Retrieval-Oriented Design Choices Illustrated by the Voynich Manuscript

detail.title: A Tutorial on Cognitive Optimization in External Memory Systems: Reinterpreting Stolfi's Layers and Currier's Partitions as Retrieval-Oriented Design Choices Illustrated by the Voynich Manuscript
detail.abstract: In the companion tutorial (Durdanovic, 2026), Bayesian model selection under a strict Zero-Patch Standard strongly favored a Structured Reference System (H r e f) over natural language (H lang) or conventional cipher hypotheses for the Voynich Manuscript(VMS). This paper addresses the consequent mechanism: what cognitive pressures plausibly led a 15th-century author to construct a text with rigid morphology, high type-level uniqueness, and sectional vocabulary disjointness? We argue that the field requires a high-level course correction: moving from postulating linguistic priors to deducing the system's purpose from its apparent anomalies. We reinterpret Stolfi's crustmantle-core decomposition and Currier's sectional partitions not as linguistic failures, but as cognitive optimizations for manual retrieval in an external memory system. We explicitly derive the Positional Coding of glyphs (rigid slots) as a "visual combination lock" designed to exploit parallel feature binding [17, 18]. The VMS is thus interpreted as a paper-based external memory artifact-a specialized reference book designed to offload complex domain knowledge while preserving low-error lookup under manual search constraints.

detail.abstract: Allocating limited water resources among competing uses is increasingly challenging as climate variability intensifies. Water is typically allocated through administrative rules rather than markets, yet the implicit priorities that guide these decisions are rarely observed or quantified, making it difficult to evaluate whether non-market allocation approximates efficient outcomes. We develop a structural framework to recover these priorities from observed management behavior. We model the planner's problem as a stochastic dynamic optimization and use the simulated method of moments to estimate preference weights that rationalize historical storage and release patterns. Applied to the Panama Canal Watershed-a multipurpose system supporting navigation, hydropower, and municipal supply-we find that drinking-water reliability and upstream storage management receive the highest priority, while hydropower serves as a flexible adjustment margin. Counterfactual simulations suggest that administrative allocation can broadly serve competing water uses without large reductions in aggregate value, but sustained drought forces increasingly costly trade-offs.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how population dynamics and a recoverable resource jointly constrain long-run sustainability in a continuous-time planner model. Output combines capital with a CES aggregate of labour and recoverable resource services, so the elasticity of substitution between population and the resource becomes a structural parameter. The resource regenerates but may collapse under sustained overuse, while the planner chooses fertility and resource-saving effort subject to a lower bound on per capita consumption. We first characterize a viability region: the set of initial conditions and admissible controls from which consumption can be kept above the floor while the resource remains above collapse. We then derive an optimal sustainability corridor, defined as the subset of the viability region that satisfies the planner's first-order conditions and therefore constitutes welfare-maximizing sustainable trajectories. This distinction separates technological-demographic feasibility from optimal policy choice. The analysis yields sharp threshold results. There exists a maximum sustainable population that depends on the elasticity of substitution, critical bounds on fertility below which sustainability is possible, and a joint necessity of demographic control, resource-saving effort, and substitution capacity. The framework provides a unified dynamic characterization of population-resource interactions in which viability constraints and optimal control jointly determine long-run sustainability.

The methodology integrates value chain theory, structured finance principles, institutional economics, and distributed ledger technology into a unified framework for engineering digital economic constructions.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of legal and regulatory frameworks on foreign investor protection and capital market development in Nigeria between 2020 and 2024. The research analyzes key market indicators, including market capitalization, domestic participation, and foreign investor activity, to evaluate how regulatory structures influence investor confidence and market growth. Findings from the study indicate that while the Nigerian capital market experienced growth in overall market capitalization and increased domestic participation, foreign investor participation remained relatively low and inconsistent throughout the study period. title: Parallel Capitalism: The Financial Power and Economic Structure of Organized Crime in Brazil

detail.title: Parallel Capitalism: The Financial Power and Economic Structure of Organized Crime in Brazil
detail.abstract: This paper examines the growing financial and structural power of organized crime in Brazil, analyzing how criminal factions such as the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Comando Vermelho (CV), and Terceiro Comando Puro (TCP) have evolved into diversified economic conglomerates. Based on the compilation and crossreferencing of official, academic, and journalistic sources, the study estimates that the criminal economy moves between R$160 and R$200 billion annually, an amount equivalent to the GDP of countries such as Croatia or Paraguay. The research reveals that only 15% of this revenue derives from drug trafficking, while 85% originates from legal or semi-formal activities such as betting, logistics, construction, real estate, fuel, and fintech operations. This diversification marks a new stage in criminal economics-the transition from local gangs to illicit corporate structures endowed with capital reserves, credit networks, and governance systems. The findings suggest that Brazil's organized crime operates today as a parallel economic system, with market-like characteristics, institutional rationality, and measurable macroeconomic impact. The paper introduces the concept of "Parallel Capitalism," defined as the coexistence between formal and criminal economies that collectively sustain consumption, employment, and informal credit flows in marginalized territories.

detail.abstract: Public R&D support attracts both academic and practical attention. Recent studies investigate the combination of different R&D policy instruments (policy mix), focusing on R&D subsidies and tax credits ("hard support"), despite the variety of actual instruments covering "soft support," such as matching, mediation, and consultation services. Moreover, despite the decentralization of R&D policies in several countries, few studies have addressed place-based (city-level) R&D support with a variety of policy instruments. This study fills these gaps by estimating the effects of the local R&D policy mix, covering both hard and soft instruments, based on unique panel data of 146 Japanese cities for 18 years. Using panel fixed-effects estimations, we find that hard support has positive and significant effects on patent applications per person, while soft support significantly increases productivity. Finally, the coefficient of the interaction term of hard and soft support, estimated by the system GMM, suggests their complementarity.

detail.abstract: This article advances a new perspective on corporate purpose, grounded in the institutional conditions under which corporate privileges are granted. Using a novel dataset of historical UK royal charters and a mixed-methods empirical strategy, the study shows that early corporations articulated specific, enforceable, and public facing purpose clauses because incorporation was a scarce privilege that allowed the Crown to impose obligations as a “asking price” for the benefits of the corporate form. Machine-learning evidence demonstrates that clauses reflecting Crown leverage cluster systematically and decline over time as incorporation becomes more accessible. The findings reframe corporate purpose not merely as a normative contest among stakeholders but as the product of institutional bargaining at the point of corporate formation, offering a historical lens for contemporary purpose debates.
