detail.abstract:
This study examines the financial performance of selected Pan-African banks over the period 2018–2023. It aims to assess how effectively banks across different regions of Africa have utilized their assets and equity to generate profitability. The analysis focuses on key performance indicators, specifically Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE), using data from four major banks representing West, East, Southern, and North Africa.

The study adopts a comparative analytical approach, with the period divided into pre-COVID-19 (2018–2019), COVID-19 (2020–2021), and post-COVID-19 (2022–2023) phases to evaluate performance under varying economic conditions.

The findings reveal significant regional differences in financial performance. Commercial International Bank (North Africa) demonstrated the strongest and most consistent profitability, while banks in East and West Africa showed steady performance and resilience over time. In contrast, Standard Bank (Southern Africa) recorded comparatively lower overall profitability despite some improvement.

Overall, the results highlight the resilience and adaptability of African banks, as well as the varying efficiency in resource utilization across regions. The study contributes to understanding regional performance dynamics and provides insights for investors and policymakers interested in the African banking sector.

title: U.S. Bank Stock Crashes: Signals, Nonlinearities, and Regime Dependence
affiliations: , University of New Orleans - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics and Finance, Marquette University - Department of Finance, University of New Orleans - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics and Finance and University of New Orleans

detail.title: U.S. Bank Stock Crashes: Signals, Nonlinearities, and Regime Dependence
detail.abstract: We study the real-time prediction of bank stock crashes using a daily panel of 106 U.S. commercial banks over 2010-2024 (230,134 bank-day observations). Accounting fundamentals do not deteriorate before crashes: none of five key indicators moves differentially in crash quarters (smallest p = 0.18), and linear model coefficients reverse sign across bank types and size categories. We benchmark nine prediction models in rolling-origin evaluation and find that a simple 22-day realized volatility signal is statistically indistinguishable from XGBoost and spline-logistic specifications (DeLong p = 0.75-0.97). Using SHAP analysis as an econometric diagnostic, we identify specific nonlinear thresholds equity ratios below 9% and held-to-maturity securities exposure that interact with stablecoin market stress to amplify crash risk. As supplementary evidence, we exploit difference-indifferences around stablecoin stress episodes: HTM-to-equity is the primary amplifier (β =-0.019, p = 0.006), while uninsured deposit concentration shows only marginal effects (p = 0.093). Risk drivers shift across regimes: pre-COVID predictions rely on return volatility, while post-COVID models weight funding structure (Spearman ρ of feature importance drops from 0.60 to 0.40). At a 1% investigation budget, a parametric interaction model achieves 22.9% precision, outperforming all ML alternatives.

title: The Limit of Financialization: Phase Transitions in Asset Pricing and the Terminal Cash Constraint

detail.title: The Limit of Financialization: Phase Transitions in Asset Pricing and the Terminal Cash Constraint
detail.abstract: This paper models advanced financialization as a metastable asset-pricing regime sustained by leverage-amplified liquidity. Departing from standard equilibrium-adjustment frameworks, we conceptualize asset pricing as a critical system whose stability depends on the elasticity of effective liquidity. We introduce the Liquidity Dominance Hypothesis (LDH), utilizing Landau's theory of phase transitions to demonstrate that when liquidity elasticity falls below a structural threshold, the pricing mechanism undergoes a discontinuous regime shift-from a leverage-dominant equilibrium to a cash-constrained settlement regime, defined as the Terminal Cash Constraint. The model predicts that such transitions are preceded by Critical Slowing Down (diverging variance and autocorrelation), a phenomenon consistent with historical liquidity crises. We argue that historical restorations of liquidity (e.g., 2008, 2020) represent successful stabilizations of the metastable state, but do not falsify the existence of the terminal constraint where restoration mechanisms fail.

title: The Roles of Big Data in Building Performance: A Function of Relationships and Contexts

detail.title: The Roles of Big Data in Building Performance: A Function of Relationships and Contexts
detail.abstract: This study investigates how big data contributes to performance in organizations. This study employed an integrative literature review method to construct knowledge about performance in organizations concerning the use of big data and the implementation of big data analytics. This article synthesized knowledge about how big data enhances performance. This article establishes that performance is the quality of functioning that is a key determinant of organizational success or failure. Based on the findings from the synthesized literature, this article proposes that performance is a function of relationships and contexts. Essentially, the relationship between big data, big data analytics, and requisite big data analytics capabilities that include level of knowledge, level of skills, sensing, seizing, transforming, tangible resources, and intangible resources is crucial in building various types of performance and there are varying contextual factors regulating the relationships. Big data on its own is not sufficient in bringing about the desired performance, but a combination of processes for storing, acquiring, processing, analyzing, and interpreting big data in conjunction with the competencies or resources for big data analytics is required. This article emphasizes that the big data-performance connection is dependent on big data analytics processes, requisite big data analytics capabilities, the generation of valuable insights or knowledge, the capacity for data and analytics to enhance decision-making, and the creation of value and competitive advantage through insight-backed decision-making. In addition, this article highlights further research problems for the research community to address and provides useful recommendations for implementation by practitioners.

title: Leadership Scorecard(The Leadership Scorecard is part of the article titled: Leadership in the era of Digital Transformation: The Digital Leadership Approaches)

detail.title: Leadership Scorecard(The Leadership Scorecard is part of the article titled: Leadership in the era of Digital Transformation: The Digital Leadership Approaches)
detail.abstract: The digital era has heralded changes in the business environment that consequently transformed the understanding of leadership because technological advancement and digitalization place extra demands on organizational leaders. In exploring the concept of leadership in the digital age, this study employed an integrative literature review method. The article establishes that successful digital leadership depends on the transformational leadership approach. Successful digital leadership is contingent on the leader’s ability to inspire, motivate, build relationships, collaborate, generate ideas, and model requisite behaviours toward the attainment of organization goals. The findings from this review indicate that digital leadership is crucial to the outcomes of an organization such as innovation, problem-solving, digital transformation, organizational performance, growth, and sustainability. At the same time, the effectiveness of digital leadership depends on the success of digital transformation, innovation, organizational performance, and growth. Achieving effective digital leadership necessitates that leaders employ a combination of approaches, which this article described under the concept of the digital leadership system. This article proposes the digital leadership system (DLS) which encompasses the ideas that successfully leading digital enterprises, digital transformation, and digital or technological innovations require a future-oriented approach and timely positioning of the business, navigating self and people, tracking performance, and mapping data, and driving growth and innovation to achieve the three- dimensional sustainability outcomes. The article highlights the critical expectations for leadership under each approach and broadened the knowledge about leadership in the digital era by presenting the definitions of digital leadership. In addition, valuable ideas are discussed for supporting successful real-world practice of digital leadership and areas of further research useful in advancing knowledge about digital leadership are outlined.

title: Beyond the Firm: Intrapreneurs with Entrepreneurial Intentions and Informal Investment Roles
affiliations: Columbia University - Graduate School of Arts and Sciences

detail.title: Beyond the Firm: Intrapreneurs with Entrepreneurial Intentions and Informal Investment Roles
detail.abstract: While existing research on intrapreneurs primarily studies them through the lens of firms, this study examines their role in the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. Using data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (2015 to 2017) across 75 countries and territories, we apply fixed and mixed effects models and find that intrapreneurs are more likely than non-intrapreneurs to have entrepreneurial intentions and to engage in informal investment. Deeper involvement in intrapreneurial activities—such as initiating projects, participating in multiple phases of intrapreneurship, and assuming leadership roles—strengthens these associations. Additionally, while the results are not consistently significant across all models, there is some evidence that when intrapreneurial projects are seen as high-growth, individuals may be less inclined to pursue independent entrepreneurship but more likely to invest informally. Cross-country analysis reveals significant variation in the effects of intrapreneurship on entrepreneurial intentions and informal investment. As the effects are positive and significant for most countries, the variation exists primarily in their magnitude. Multilevel models show that access to formal financing, in the form of bank loans and venture capital, explains part of this heterogeneity. These findings suggest that intrapreneurship may stimulate broader entrepreneurial activity, offering valuable insights for policymakers seeking to foster entrepreneurial ecosystems, and for managers wishing to retain intrapreneurial talent.

title: Administrative Precedent as a Governance Tool in Competition Law Enforcement: A Comparative Analysis of EU, US, and UK Practice

detail.title: Administrative Precedent as a Governance Tool in Competition Law Enforcement: A Comparative Analysis of EU, US, and UK Practice
detail.abstract: Competition authorities exercise broad administrative discretion in defining infringement standards, calibrating sanctions, and managing doctrinal evolution. This article examines administrative precedent as a governance and communication tool that structures such discretion without foreclosing necessary adaptation. Drawing on comparative analysis of enforcement practice in the European Union, the United States, and the United Kingdom, the article demonstrates that structured engagement with prior decisions enhances enforcement credibility, strengthens deterrence, and improves the consistency of judicial review outcomes. Three institutional mechanisms receive sustained attention: reason giving as a discipline on discretion; transparency in sanctioning practice; and the explicit management of doctrinal change.

title: Government Startup Grants as Informational Signals: Causal Evidence from Fiscal-Year Timing
affiliations: Bar Ilan University, New York University (NYU) - New York University and Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Department of Economics

detail.title: Government Startup Grants as Informational Signals: Causal Evidence from Fiscal-Year Timing
detail.abstract: Financial reporting by early-stage ventures provides limited information to outside investors: revenues and profits are uncommon, intangible assets are underrepresented, and human capital is unrecognized, weakening traditional accounting-based signals. This paper studies government startup grants as an external disclosure signal that supplements early-stage ventures sparse financial reporting. Drawing on signalling theory, we argue that grant approval conveys third-party validation that is observable, credible, and costly to obtain. To identify the causal effect of grant receipt, we exploit quasi-random variation in approval likelihood induced by fiscal-year budgeting cycles. Startups applying early in the fiscal year, particularly in January, face higher approval rates due to renewed public funding availability. We use application timing as an instrument for grant receipt in a two-stage least squares framework. The results show that grant receipt, rather than the monetary value of the grant, significantly increases the probability of a successful IPO. These findings indicate that the primary economic role of government grants in capital markets operates through signalling channels, via certification and visibility, rather than through direct financial support.

title: AI Washing: Strategic Disclosure and Backlash
affiliations: University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh - Business School, University of Edinburgh and University of Edinburgh

detail.title: AI Washing: Strategic Disclosure and Backlash
detail.abstract: As firms increasingly exaggerate artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in disclosures, we analyze market responses to unsubstantiated AI claims. Using BERT-based text classification and AI patent data for U.S. firms (2018-2023), we find that such narratives initially attract investors but ultimately yield negative market reactions and sustained underperformance. Results demonstrate market penalties for AI overclaiming through both short-term investor responses and long-term operational outcomes, extending narrative economics to emerging technologies. The study highlights that while narratives can mobilize attention, markets ultimately punish rhetoric that outpaces implementation.

title: Institutional Complementarities and Frictions Between Public and Private Antitrust Enforcement

detail.title: Institutional Complementarities and Frictions Between Public and Private Antitrust Enforcement
detail.abstract: The expansion of private antitrust enforcement has been widely promoted as a means of strengthening deterrence and complementing public prosecution. Much of the existing debate, however, evaluates private enforcement primarily in terms of enforcement intensity, paying limited attention to how private litigation interacts institutionally with public enforcement mechanisms. This article develops a general institutional framework for analyzing the interaction between public and private antitrust enforcement across jurisdictions. The analysis shows that the welfare effects of private enforcement depend less on its volume than on its alignment with the incentives, information, and discretion of public authorities. Within this framework, private enforcement enhances welfare when it improves detection or compensation without increasing expected legal error or undermining public cooperation incentives. Conversely, when private litigation distorts enforcement priorities or weakens institutional screening, expanded private enforcement may reduce welfare even if deterrence rises. By shifting the focus from enforcement intensity to institutional alignment, the article provides a framework applicable to both developed and developing jurisdictions, particularly those facing resource constraints or institutional asymmetries. The analysis contributes to the law and economics literature on enforcement design and offers guidance for policymakers reconsidering the balance between public prosecution and private litigation in diverse institutional environments.

title: Learning to Automate: How Multi-Site Firms Distribute Exploration and Exploitation Across Facilities
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - College of Engineering and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Learning to Automate: How Multi-Site Firms Distribute Exploration and Exploitation Across Facilities
detail.abstract: The exploration-exploitation framework has shaped decades of research on organizational learning, but it has focused primarily on what organizations learn about-new products, markets, and technologies for external value creation. We extend the framework to a different problem: how organizations manage learning itself when improving internal operations. Adopting a new practice requires costly exploration before efficient exploitation becomes possible, yet operations must continue. How do organizations absorb learning costs without disrupting ongoing work? We argue that multi-unit organizations solve this by distributing learning across units: some units bear the costs of exploration while others capture the benefits of exploitation, with knowledge flowing between them. Using daily operational data from eleven distribution centers, 59,021 worker separations, and 69 interviews at a U.S. logistics firm implementing automation-with corroborating qualitative evidence from a second large multi-site firm-we show that managers deliberately assign facilities to different learning roles. Pilot sites absorb exploration costs, while scale and optimization sites exploit proven practices. Pooling facilities produces a misleading picture of “failure”; disaggregating by role reveals systematic variation reflecting the organization learning as designed. We contribute a theory of distributed learning for multi-unit organizations and a new explanation for heterogeneous outcomes in practice adoption.

title: The Valuation Invariant: Why Your Spreadsheet Is Telling You a Story - And How to Know When to Trust It​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

detail.title: The Valuation Invariant: Why Your Spreadsheet Is Telling You a Story - And How to Know When to Trust It​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
detail.abstract: Standard valuation models-DCF, CAPM, multiples-treat variance as noise to be minimized or risk to be discounted. They have no built-in mechanism for detecting when a system has left its stable operating window. This paper offers a different lens. Drawing on the Coordination Invariant (S = C/V), we propose that the ratio's predictive behavior is determined by shock type: in variance shocks, high-constraint systems demonstrate resilience; in medium shocks, high constraint becomes liability. This is not a better calculator. It is a different lens. Lenses do not replace tools. They tell you which tool to use when.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning vs. Classical Models for High-Volatility Agricultural Commodities

detail.title: A Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning vs. Classical Models for High-Volatility Agricultural Commodities
detail.abstract: Price volatility in agriculture creates significant economic uncertainty, necessitating robust forecasting frameworks for effective market planning. This study presents a comparative analysis of statistical and deep learning architectures for predicting tomato prices in Karnataka, India. We evaluate the performance of classical models (ARIMA, NNAR, and Prophet) against deep learning approaches (LSTM and MLP) using standardized error metrics, including MSE, MAPE, RMSE, and MAE. Our findings demonstrate that the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network outperformed other models in capturing non-linear trends, achieving a MAPE of 11.65%. Notably, while the Prophet model struggled with historical price anomalies, the integration of anomaly detection significantly improved its fit. The optimized LSTM model was subsequently utilized to generate a 3-month forward forecast. The results underscore the transformative potential of artificial intelligence in automating agricultural market intelligence and enhancing predictive accuracy for stakeholders.

title: The Missing Cases: Student Loan Discharge in Bankruptcy After Reform
affiliations: University of Michigan Law School, University of California, Irvine School of Law and Howard University School of Law

detail.title: The Missing Cases: Student Loan Discharge in Bankruptcy After Reform

detail.abstract: Despite the 2022 DOJ Guidance designed to make student loan discharge in bankruptcy more accessible, barely any borrowers are using it. Using hand-coded court records from 240 cases, AI-assisted classification of case outcomes, credit bureau records, and a survey of 127 bankruptcy attorneys, we investigate why. Two intertwined problems emerge. First, the odds are worse than advertised: only about 56% of cases achieve full or partial discharge, far below the government's claimed success rate. Second, the process is expensive: attorneys typically charge thousands of dollars in flat fees, and 63% report that they cannot find clients who can afford to pay. We propose practical reforms (including better outcome data, standardized procedures, and alternative fee structures) that could expand access to student loan relief in bankruptcy without new legislation.

title: PF Efficiency Index (PFEI): A Nonlinear Efficiency Metric for Trading Systems

detail.abstract: The PF Efficiency Index (PFEI) is introduced as a nonlinear diagnostic metric for assessing the structural efficiency and robustness of discretionary and algorithmic trading systems, where “PF” refers to the system’s profit factor. Instead of evaluating performance only via headline figures such as profit factor and win rate, PFEI explicitly incorporates trade win rate, tick win rate, and the length of loss sequences to distinguish between healthy and overstretched performance profiles. Using grid-based parameter studies and Monte Carlo simulations, the paper illustrates how seemingly similar profit factors can arise from fundamentally different structural configurations, leading to very different levels of fragility. The proposed framework classifies systems into qualitative efficiency zones and is intended as a practical tool for traders and system developers to evaluate and compare trading systems beyond conventional metrics.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure, State Capacity, and Decentralisation: Rethinking Local Governance in India

detail.title: Digital Public Infrastructure, State Capacity, and Decentralisation: Rethinking Local Governance in India
detail.abstract: India's approach to decentralised governance has evolved through a long process of institutional reforms, resulting in the constitutional recognition of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies, because of which a formal structure of decentralisation is now firmly in place across both rural and urban governance systems. But, efficient functioning of the local institutions still remains as an unresolved issue despite such structures. There is a huge gap between the responsibilities allotted to the local bodies and their effective execution. These differences are observed within both Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies, indicating that the problem is structural than sectoral. The inefficiency of local governance is primarily driven by three factors: limited administrative capacities, lack of fiscal autonomy and fragmented institutional cooperation. These challenges, are usually explained in terms of inadequate financial resources. According to the evidence, graver problems lie in the limited seat capacity at the local levels, especially in the ability of the institutions to manage information, coordinate multiple function and ensure accountability in implementation. Also, the formal decentralisation of authority has failed to produce reliable gains in service quality or institutional efficiency. Thus, the rise of Digital Public Infrastructure now adds a transformative new element to the governance debate. Systems based on digital identity, payments and data exchange have demonstrated their ability to improve public service delivery at larger scale. This paper therefore examines the relationship between decentralisation and state capacity by situating digital systems within the broader evolution of local governance. It brings three key elements together: the development of decentralised institutions, the operational constraints faced by them and the growing role of digital infrastructure. The core argument is that strengthening local governance needs a shift in focus from formal institutional structure to the development of functional capacity. Since Digital Public Infrastructure acts as a foundational layer in this framework, it is guaranteed that it will support effective government. However, its impact would depend on multiple factors such as access to digital systems, institutional readiness and broader administrative environment in which local bodies operate.

title: The Impact of Abolishing the Gift and Inheritance Tax on Firm Strategic Decisions and Outcomes: The Case of Sweden
affiliations: University of Melbourne,  and Stockholm School of Economics

detail.title: The Impact of Abolishing the Gift and Inheritance Tax on Firm Strategic Decisions and Outcomes: The Case of Sweden
detail.abstract: Current debates on the gift and inheritance tax are often ideological, and empirical evidence on the effects of this tax on the strategic decision-making of owners of privately owned companies is scarce. To better understand the economic and societal consequences of gift and inheritance taxes, this white paper uses population data on private companies in Sweden to examine how privately owned companies were affected by the abolition of the gift and inheritance tax in 2004/2005. We applied a matching technique to compare privately-owned companies led by owner-managers who have potential next-generation successors in their family (treated group) to childless owner-managers without potential next-generation successors (control group), thereby drawing on a sample of approximately 37,000 companies. We found that the abolition of the tax increased net sales, profitability, fixed and current assets, and productivity of private firms.  The tax abolition thus appears to have incentivized and enabled stronger growth and earnings power for private firms that had the prospect of being handed over to the next generation. The increased earnings power of these firms thereby appears to be enabled by the abolished need for companies to extract capital through dividends to pay future gift and inheritance taxes, as we found that the tax abolition resulted in increased liquidity and shareholders’ equity, while reducing leverage. Our study also points to long-term benefits to society from these increases in earnings power as we found that the reform resulted in higher corporate income taxes paid among firms with potential successors. The abolition of the gift and inheritance tax thus incurred a strengthening of recurring tax revenues from these firms. Beyond corporate tax revenues, our findings further show that firms with potential successors expanded their total salary expenditures following the reform—pointing to broader labor market benefits in payroll tax revenues and social contributions. Overall, we conclude that the abolition of the gift and inheritance tax in Sweden encouraged and enabled firms with potential next generation owners to adopt a long-term horizon, be growth-oriented, and to create transgenerational value, which in turn benefitted society by increasing recurring corporate tax revenues and employee salaries—suggesting the reform’s positive consequences extended beyond the firms themselves.

title: E-Waste in India: Challenges, Policies and Economic Perspectives

detail.title: E-Waste in India: Challenges, Policies and Economic Perspectives
detail.abstract: This paper discusses the emerging issue of e-waste generation in India from an economic point of view. With the increasing pace of urbanization and technological development, major cities in India have experienced a substantial increase in electronic waste. This paper relies on secondary data sources, including government publications and research papers, to discuss state-wise and city-wise e-waste generation. The results show that industrialized and urbanized states generate the highest amount of e-waste due to increased consumption and reduced product life cycles. This paper also describes e-waste as a market failure problem, which generates negative externalities with social costs exceeding private costs. To overcome these issues, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) policies have been implemented by the government. This paper concludes that successful implementation of policies and awareness among people are required for effective e-waste management in India.

title: Stable Matchings with Choice Correspondences under Acyclicity
affiliations: Indian Statistical Institute, New Delhi - Indian Statistical Innstitute, Delhi Cente , New Delhi, Ashoka University - Department of Economics and Shiv Nadar University

detail.title: Stable Matchings with Choice Correspondences under Acyclicity
detail.abstract: We study the existence of stable matchings when agents have choice correspondences instead of preference relations. We extend the framework of Chambers and Yenmez (2017) by weakening the Path Independence assumption. For many-tomany markets, we show that stable matchings exist when choice correspondences satisfy Substitutability and a new General Acyclicity condition. We provide a constructive proof using a Grow or Discard Algorithm that iteratively expands or eliminates contracts until a strongly maximal Individually Rational set is reached. We provide an algorithm to obtain stable matchings in which rejected contracts are not permanently discarded, distinguishing our approach significantly from standard DAA-type algorithms. For one-to-one markets, we show that Path Independence alone does not guarantee stability. We introduce a replacement-based notion of stability and provide an algorithm that constructs stable matchings when choice correspondences satisfy Binary Acyclicity.

title:

A Case Study of the Philippines Energy System

detail.title:
A Universal Dynamic Balance-feedback Framework for Resource Depletion, Energy Transition, and Socioeconomic Stability
A Case Study of the Philippines Energy System
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a unified dynamic balance-feedback framework grounded in four universal systemic laws-the Law of System Integrity, the Universal Law of Balance in Nature, the Universal Feedback Loop Mechanism, and the Universal Interconnected Nodes-to describe how global and regional energy systems respond to finite resource constraints. Drawing on real historical oil data for both the global market and the Philippines (1980-2022), and on a numerically solved simulation model calibrated specifically to Philippine conditions, we show that sustained imbalance triggers measurable corrective feedback leading the system toward a new equilibrium characterised by higher renewable-technology adoption and lower fossil-fuel dependence. Policy implications for the Philippines Department of Energy's National Renewable Energy Program (NREP) are discussed, and model limitations are acknowledged explicitly.

detail.abstract: When states confront credible evidence of historical wrongdoing, some governing elites engage; others deny, deflect, and attack. This article argues that the difference is simultaneously moral and structural: governing elites vary in identity-threat tolerance, the capacity to process disconfirming evidence without ego-defensive distortion, and democratic electoral competition creates incentive structures that systematically disadvantage that capacity. Moments of historical accountability function as natural stress-tests of this variable because they combine maximal identity threat with minimal electoral reward for candor, making behavioral patterns associated with broader governance impairment visible in the public record. The article develops the Identity-Threat Responsiveness Typology (ITRT), a set of behavioral signatures observable in elite discourse under accountability pressure, and grounds the normative implication in multiple theories of democratic legitimacy: when governing elites exhibit recurrent defensive behavioral patterns under accountability pressure, they structurally impair the contestation that legitimate governance requires.

title: Selective Recall and the Story-Statistics Gap in Stock Market Misreaction

detail.title: Selective Recall and the Story-Statistics Gap in Stock Market Misreaction
detail.abstract: I document a strong story-statistics gap in stock market misreaction to corporate news: whereas qualitative announcements exhibit mild overreaction, quantitative announcements generate pronounced underreaction. This pattern cannot be fully explained by signal-strength uncertainty, diagnostic expectations, news sentiment, or investor attention. Motivated by experimental evidence on selective recall, I hypothesize that memory evaluates similarity based on different characteristics for stories and for statistics. I propose that stories are similar within each news category due to shared narrative features, while statistics with comparable stock price impact are similar across news categories due to their numerical precision. Model-predicted misreactions under my hypothesized similarity patterns strongly align with the empirically observed story-statistics gap across news categories. I additionally find strong, measurement error-free support for my model in announcement-level data.

title: A Policy-Related Reporting Change, not Increasing Financial Distress, Drove the Late 2025 / Early 2026 Increase in the FHA Serious Delinquency Rate

detail.title: A Policy-Related Reporting Change, not Increasing Financial Distress, Drove the Late 2025 / Early 2026 Increase in the FHA Serious Delinquency Rate
detail.abstract:
The 90D+ delinquency (DQ) rate on loans insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), which captures loans that are 90 or more days delinquent but not in foreclosure or bankruptcy, increased sharply, from 3.57% in September 2025 to 5.23% in January 2026, an increase of 1.66 percentage points (pp) in just 4 months. Market commentators have cited this sharp increase in the FHA 90D+ DQ rate as a sign of financial stress among FHA borrowers. However, we find that 92% (1.53pp) of the increase in the FHA 90D+ DQ rate is driven by how an FHA policy change is reported rather than increasing financial fragility among FHA borrowers.

Beginning in October 2025, FHA began requiring Trial Payment Plans (TPPs) for borrowers entering a home retention option. Rather than transitioning directly to current after entering the home retention option, as had previously been FHA’s practice, borrowers must now make 3 consecutive payments before their loan is marked current. Therefore, loans are now classified as 90D+ DQ for at least 3 additional months, which creates a corresponding increase in the FHA 90D+ DQ rate.

Absent the reporting change, the FHA 90D+ DQ rate would have increased modestly in late 2025 / early 2026, to 3.70% in January 2026, an increase of just 0.13%. The 1.53pp “TPP gap”– the difference between the reported rate and our revision that removes the impact of the policy-driven reporting change – will persist. Therefore, any comparisons of FHA 90D+ DQ rates across the October 2025 TPP-policy implementation threshold should be adjusted accordingly. TPPs are an important improvement in the FHA home retention program, as they allow the borrower to demonstrate that the provided solution is affordable before it is made permanent and FHA absorbs the cost. Therefore, the impact of the TPP requirement on FHA’s 90D+ DQ rate should not be misinterpreted—FHA loan performance has been remarkably stable over the last 12 months.

title: LLM-Based Expectations and Fed Communication
affiliations: University of Houston - C.T. Bauer College of Business, , Wuhan University and Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: LLM-Based Expectations and Fed Communication
detail.abstract: We introduce a new approach to measuring monetary policy surprises in FOMC press conferences. Our method uses LLMs to generate counterfactual press-conference responses by the Federal Reserve Chair and measures policy surprises as deviations between realized and simulated answers. Using high-frequency intraday data from 2011 to 2025, we show that equity prices respond strongly to these surprises: hawkish surprises lead to significant declines in stock prices, while dovish surprises increase prices. Importantly, markets respond to the unexpected component of communication rather than to the level of expressed policy stance. Heterogeneity tests show that market responses to policy surprises operate through expectation formation and belief updating. Reactions are strongest when the Chair's answers directly inform the future policy path, namely for forwardlooking, policy-related, or statement-linked questions, and are larger, though slower to emerge, during periods of elevated market uncertainty. Responses are also stronger following dovish FOMC statements, when prior expectations are less anchored. Finally, omitting macroeconomic context or the policy statement from the LLM prompt eliminates the return predictability of policy surprises. Our findings demonstrate that LLMs provide a powerful tool for identifying economically meaningful surprises in real-time policy communication.

title: Bubbles, Speculation and Crises: Financial Instability and Fraud, 1800-2015
affiliations: University of Leeds - Faculty of Business

detail.title: Bubbles, Speculation and Crises: Financial Instability and Fraud, 1800-2015
detail.abstract: The paper examines whether market instability creates fraud opportunity and if so, how? To do so, it investigates the long-run relationship between financial instability, speculative behaviour, and fraud in Britain from the early nineteenth century to the post-2008 era. Drawing on a newly constructed speculation-related fraud (SRF) index based on historical newspaper reporting, it demonstrates that periods of abundant credit, market exuberance, and weak regulation generated opportunities for financial deception in the middle decades of the nineteenth century. During this period, financial instability prompted moral criticism of speculation, emphasising its relationship to fraud, and was weaponised by political opposition to frontier investment projects in a time of rapid economic development. Structural changes after 1870 dampened speculation and related fraud for over a century. An apparent resurgence after 1990 did not match the excesses of the early Victorian period and speculative risk became more effectively encapsulated in innovative financial products. Together, these cycles show how changing financial structures shaped the prevalence and character of speculative fraud.

title: Institutional Timing, Renewal Risk, and the Political Economy of Drought Governance

detail.title: Institutional Timing, Renewal Risk, and the Political Economy of Drought Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Non

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural theory of duration misalignment in rule-based crisis finance under recurrent climatic shocks. In drought systems, ecological recovery duration (Tr) often exceeds authorization validity duration (Tv) for contingent credit lines, crisis windows, and parametric facilities. When Tr exceeds Tv, institutional design mechanically generates repeated mandatory expiry nodes prior to stabilization. Each expiry constitutes a rule-bound renewal decision. The core claim is architectural rather than behavioral. Emergency persistence is typically attributed to climate volatility, fiscal scarcity, or political opportunism. This paper advances a distinct structural hypothesis: recurrence may arise from deterministic properties of authorization cadence itself. When recovery time systematically outlasts validation intervals, repetition is embedded in institutional timing architecture. Temporal misalignment is formalized through the Recovery-Validation Ratio (RVR = Tr divided by Tv). Its integer component, E equal to floor(RVR), measures the number of mandatory expiry exposures implied before ecological recovery. E is mechanically generated by the interaction of ecological duration and statutory authorization cycles. The Institutional Timing Theorem shows that cumulative reactivation probability increases monotonically with expiry exposure. If p_k denotes renewal probability at expiry node k, the probability of at least one reactivation across E exposures equals one minus the product over k of (1 minus p_k). Whenever renewal probability at any node is positive, cumulative renewal risk rises strictly with E. This result follows from repeated renewal opportunities embedded in institutional rules and does not depend on funding scale, drought frequency, or bureaucratic incentives. The theorem yields a falsifiable implication: the marginal effect of expiry exposure on renewal probability must be positive, conditional on ecological severity and macroeconomic risk. Absence of such an effect rejects the structural timing mechanism. Empirically, the paper integrates formal derivation, measurement of ecological recovery using satellite-derived NDVI intervals (2000-2025), documentation-based measures of authorization duration, and estimation within a discrete-time hazard framework in which renewal events occur exclusively at expiry nodes. Exposure count derived from RVR enters as the central structural regressor alongside controls for drought severity, macroeconomic stress, institutional fixed effects, and baseline duration dependence. Tests of monotonicity, convexity, and entrenchment evaluate whether renewal hazard accelerates with accumulated exposure. The contribution is structural: crisis finance is modeled as a time-structured institutional process rather than solely a funding mechanism. By linking ecological recovery dynamics, rule-bound authorization cadence, and renewal hazard within a unified and testable architecture, the paper provides a formal explanation for how temporary emergency instruments become systemically embedded when duration misalignment persists.

detail.abstract: Ontario Works (OW) is Ontario's primary income assistance program for individuals and families experiencing financial hardship who are able to participate in employment-related activities. Established under the Ontario Works Act, 1997, the program combines income support and employment assistance within a shared provincial-municipal delivery framework. Since its introduction, Ontario's housing markets, labour force structure, and broader human services systems have changed substantially. This working paper examines Ontario Works within its contemporary economic and social context. Drawing on publicly available provincial data, Statistics Canada labour force trends, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) rental market reports, and municipal housing and homelessness system planning evidence from Northern Ontario (2026-2035 planning horizon), the paper analyzes participation trends, housing affordability pressures, chronic homelessness dynamics, service acuity, and fiscal interdependencies. The analysis adopts a neutral, evidence-informed approach and situates Ontario Works within broader system interactions involving housing, health, and justice sectors. The paper contributes to ongoing policy dialogue by identifying structural considerations relevant to program responsiveness, sustainability, and cross-sector integration.

title: What Good Can "Obiter Dicta" Accomplish?-On the Privy Council's Dicta on Voidness Versus Voidability of Share Issuances for Improper Purposes in Tianrui v China Shanshui

detail.title: What Good Can "Obiter Dicta" Accomplish?-On the Privy Council's Dicta on Voidness Versus Voidability of Share Issuances for Improper Purposes in Tianrui v China Shanshui
detail.abstract: Hundreds of companies incorporated in "offshore" jurisdictions such as the Cayman Islands are listed on United States (US) stock exchanges. As foreign private issuers under US securities rules, they are exempt from most domestic US corporate governance requirements. Overseeing their corporate governance standards falls upon offshore courts and the Privy Council. The Privy Council affirmed in Tianrui v China Shanshui a shareholder's standing to bring personal claim against directors who had issued company shares to dilute the shareholder. Most commentators overlooked that the Tianrui decision contained a statement that improper share issuances are voidable but not void. Such a statement, if followed literally, would defeat a century of case law protecting shareholder voting rights, render Tianrui's own ruling circular and self-defeating, and leave corporate governance of foreign private issuers in "no man zone." This analysis establishes that the Privy Council's statement in Tianrui on void and voidability should be treated as dicta and disregarded, to safeguard more than a century of case law development protecting shareholder franchise.

title: Geopolitical Risks and Exchange Rate Volatility: Evidence from the Russia-Ukraine War

detail.title: Geopolitical Risks and Exchange Rate Volatility: Evidence from the Russia-Ukraine War
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of geopolitical risks on exchange rate volatility using the Russia-Ukraine war as a natural experiment. Employing monthly data from January 2020 to December 2024 for eight currencies, we use the Geopolitical Risk (GPR) Index developed by Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) alongside an OLS regression framework controlling for oil prices and market volatility (VIX). Our results indicate that geopolitical risk shocks significantly increase exchange rate volatility, with the effect being markedly stronger in the post-February 2022 period. Emerging market and conflict-adjacent currencies exhibit the most pronounced response. These findings carry important implications for currency risk management, central bank intervention strategies, and portfolio hedging in geopolitically uncertain environments.

title: Love me Tinder: Polarizing Effects of Alternative search Methods in Dating Market

detail.title: Love me Tinder: Polarizing Effects of Alternative search Methods in Dating Market
detail.abstract: Recent decades have seen an increase in homogamy in the US and the arrival of new internet-based search methods for relationships, but no study has explored the potential link between those two changes. Using a novel database where existing couples report their search method, I document that more attractive individuals are less likely to use alternative search mechanisms, like internet. I then build a model with heterogeneous agents and search frictions in which the search method is endogenously determined. The model indicates that the arrival of cheaper search methods leads to higher assortative matching. Empirical testing confirms these model predictions.

title: Hierarchical Modeling of Firm Heterogeneity: A Comparative Study of China and G7(2015-2024)

detail.title: Hierarchical Modeling of Firm Heterogeneity: A Comparative Study of China and G7(2015-2024)
detail.abstract: This paper develops a hierarchical modeling framework based on Maximum Likelihood Estimation (Hierarchical MLE) to analyze the temporal evolution of economic variables characterized by highly heterogeneous distributions. We apply this approach to a comparative study of major productive and technological firms across the G7 countries and China over the 2015-2024 period. The Hierarchical MLE model reveals two divergent structural power trajectories: • China as a "Dual Engine Economy": By 2023, China achieved a massive industrial power base while successfully migrating its technological fabric toward a profit structure that "mirrors" the G7's 2015 architecture. Our results demonstrate that China strategically optimized its margins-reaching a peak in 2017 arround (0.14)-to establish the financial leverage necessary to fuel this structural transition. • The G7 and Short-Cycle Decoupling: Conversely, G7 economies exhibit a structural decoupling between labor and profit within the "Short-Cycle." Labor no longer exerts a direct effect on performance; growth is now exclusively driven by the profitability of the technological "Long-Cycle" (R&D). However, the traditional industrial base remains stagnant, with the bloc progressing only through the stretching of a "hyper-efficiency" elite defined by asset intangibility.

title: Rating Agency Disagreement on Sovereign Debt Levels
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Cambridge Judge Business School, University of Cambridge - Judge Business School and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Accounting, Business Law & Taxation

detail.title: Rating Agency Disagreement on Sovereign Debt Levels

keywords: credit agency disagreement on sovereign debt

detail.abstract: Despite its importance for economic policy and capital markets, sovereign general government debt is not measured under harmonized or enforceable global accounting standards. As a result, credit rating agencies (CRAs) apply ad-hoc adjustments to transform heterogeneous fiscal data into comparable figures for rating purposes, giving rise to disagreement even over historical debt levels. Using historical debt-to-GDP figures reported by S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch for 88 countries from 2006 to 2018, we find that dispersion in CRA sovereign debt assessments is economically meaningful, averaging just over 3% of GDP. We show that this dispersion is related to features of the sovereign fiscal reporting environment. Disagreement is higher in countries with greater exposure to contingent liabilities and weaker fiscal transparency and is lower in countries subject to supranational debt rules, such as those in the European Union. Standard macroeconomic fundamentals explain relatively little of the variation in dispersion once accounting and institutional factors are considered. We further document economically significant implications. Higher dispersion is associated with more negative rating actions, and higher sovereign bond yield spreads. Consistent with the effect being driven by fiscal accounting uncertainty, these relations are present outside the global financial crisis and across economic development and institutional settings. Overall, our findings suggest that disagreement among professional intermediaries on reported debt levels conveys incremental information about fiscal transparency and uncertainty beyond headline debt measures.

title: AI-Driven Risk Management Systems In Commercial Banking

detail.abstract: The increasing complexity of financial risks in commercial banking has intensified the need for advanced, adaptive, and data-driven risk management frameworks. Global financial systems are now characterized by heightened exposure to operational disruptions, cyber threats, regulatory pressures, and evolving credit and market uncertainties. Traditional risk governance models, which rely heavily on historical data and manual processes, are increasingly inadequate in addressing real-time risk dynamics. In response, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force, enabling financial institutions to enhance predictive capabilities, automate decision-making, and strengthen resilience against systemic and operational shocks. This study aims to evaluate AI-driven risk management systems and their impact on operational resilience, regulatory compliance, and financial stability within commercial banking. The research adopts a secondary research methodology supported by a case-based analytical model, drawing insights from industry reports, empirical studies, and documented banking implementations of AI technologies. The analytical framework examines how machine learning, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation contribute to proactive risk identification and mitigation. The findings indicate that AI significantly improves predictive risk analytics, enabling early detection of financial distress and market volatility. Additionally, AI-enabled systems enhance fraud detection accuracy, optimize credit scoring models, and strengthen cybersecurity risk mitigation through real-time anomaly monitoring. These advancements support compliance with evolving regulatory requirements while reducing operational inefficiencies. The study concludes that AI serves as a strategic enabler of proactive and resilient risk governance frameworks. By integrating intelligent systems into enterprise risk management, commercial banks can enhance stability, improve decision-making, and strengthen long-term financial sustainability in an increasingly uncertain global financial environment.

title: Manufacturing Ropes of Oppression: A Feminist Analysis of the Impact of Fast Fashion on the Lives of its Female Labourers

detail.title: Manufacturing Ropes of Oppression: A Feminist Analysis of the Impact of Fast Fashion on the Lives of its Female Labourers
detail.abstract:
The fast fashion industry relies largely on the Global South as the cheap labour available in these countries aids the quick production cycles that fast fashion needs to survive. This system, however, is sustained by a fragmented garment industry, where exploitative conditions are most visible at the lower tiers of production. This paper focuses on the South Indian faction of the garment sector, and specifically targets the working conditions  and exploitation of female labourers in this industry.


While existing discussions in this arena aim to establish capitalism as the main culprit, this paper argues that these working conditions cannot be fully understood without taking into account the role of patriarchy. It draws on the Materialist Feminist theory, particularly the work of Christine Delphy, to scrutinise the way gendered divisions of labour, limited employment opportunities and deeply embedded social norms contribute to the vulnerability of the women within this industry. It also examines how these patriarchal structures shape not only workplace hierarchies and wages, but also influence the everyday lives of these women workers.


This paper endeavours to contextualise the experiences of female garment workers within a broader patriarchal framework, and move beyond the purely economic explanations. It is an attempt to highlight the ways in which gender continues to influence systems of labour and exploitation in the context of fast fashion.

title: Preventing Corruption: Ups and Downs of India's Employment Guarantee
affiliations: Ranchi University and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Preventing Corruption: Ups and Downs of India's Employment Guarantee
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines evidence of corruption in India's Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), the largest public-works programme in the world. We estimate "validation ratios", defined as the proportion of MGNREGA person-days that are reflected in independent surveys such as the National Sample Surveys and the India Human Development Survey. In the initial years of the programme, estimated validation ratios were as low as 50% or so, but they rose steadily, and by 2011-12, the bulk of MGNREGA employment was validated by two independent national surveys. The more recent Periodic Labour Force Surveys, however, suggest that validation ratios fell again after that, and may be as low as 40% or so today. In other words, MGNREGA seems to be back to square one as far as corruption is concerned. We note that PLFS data on MGNREGA may not be entirely reliable, yet the evidence of resurgent corruption is hard to dismiss. We discuss possible reasons for this setback. Briefly, MGNREGA seems to be trapped in a vicious circle of underfunding, erratic wage payments, worker discouragement and high leakages.

title: SCORE Method: A Simplified Heuristic for Pot Odds Calculation in Poker with a Built-in Conservative Edge

detail.title: SCORE Method: A Simplified Heuristic for Pot Odds Calculation in Poker with a Built-in Conservative Edge
detail.abstract: Pot odds calculation is a fundamental skill in poker, yet the conventional method requires real-time computation of ratios, fractions, and percentage comparisons under time pressure and cognitive load. This paper introduces the SCORE Method, a novel heuristic that reduces the pot odds decision to a single multiplication and a comparison against a fixed integer threshold. The method is defined as SCORE = outs × (pot/call), where a SCORE exceeding 50 on the turn (one card remaining) or 25 on the flop (two cards remaining) indicates a profitable call. We provide the algebraic derivation from classical pot odds theory, demonstrate that the thresholds are intentionally conservative, and quantify the resulting edge at approximately 1% through formal mathematical analysis and computational simulation over 10 7 randomized scenarios. The SCORE Method achieves 97.3% decision concordance with the exact method while systematically avoiding marginally profitable calls that are typically eroded by rake and variance. This heuristic represents a cognitively optimized decision tool for poker players at all levels.

detail.abstract: Recent media reports claim that Malta’s recent period of strong economic growth has rendered its economy more greenhouse-gas emissions-intensive. These conclusions are largely the product of statistical definition differences rather than a genuine deterioration in environmental performance. While Eurostat data suggest a post-2013 increase in Malta’s emissions intensity, this reflects the application of the residence principle, whereby emissions are attributed to Malta if generated by entities registered domestically, irrespective of their physical location. By contrast, emissions calculated under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, which adopts a territorial approach, show only modest growth in emissions alongside substantial economic expansion, implying continued improvements in emissions intensity. The divergence is driven mainly by international aviation linked to Malta’s fast-expanding aircraft registry. Adjusting for aviation activity occurring outside Maltese airspace reveals that Malta’s emissions intensity has continued to decline, reaching historically low levels, though challenges remain in meeting sector-specific climate targets.

title: Wakelin Melbourne Property Report 2026: Confidence and Capital Flows in Melbourne’s Investment Market

detail.title: Wakelin Melbourne Property Report 2026: Confidence and Capital Flows in Melbourne’s Investment Market
detail.abstract: Melbourne’s housing market enters 2026 at an inflection point, with a widening value gap to other Australian capitals but a fragile recovery in buyer confidence. Drawing on Wakelin Property Advisory’s proprietary enquiry microdata – a leading indicator of where serious, capitalised buyers are targeting – this report traces how investor sentiment and capital flows shifted through 2025 and what they signal for the year ahead. Investor enquiries rose 87 per cent year‑on‑year and climbed to 51 per cent of all Wakelin enquiries, while disposal enquiries fell, indicating that the land‑tax‑driven investor exodus has largely run its course. The analysis shows interstate investors moving first into Melbourne’s investment‑grade housing, followed by early signs of a local investor return, before shifting interest‑rate expectations and a February 2026 RBA rate hike unsettled confidence. Combining this microdata with external price, rental and auction series, the report examines six dynamics that will shape Melbourne’s trajectory in 2026: whether confidence consolidates or wavers, the impact of policy and politics on investor sentiment, the rent‑versus‑buy calculus, the potential for a selective apartment catch‑up, infrastructure‑driven shifts in demand, and the emerging role of AI and social platforms in property discovery.

detail.abstract: Mongolia's dependence on mineral exports left the country vulnerable to the 2012 commodity price decline, triggering a balance-of-payments crisis and fiscal distress. While initial macroeconomic easing provided temporary relief, it exacerbated public debt, weakened external balances, and eroded bank asset quality. By 2016, facing a full-blown crisis, Mongolia turned to the IMF for support. This research investigates the potential of corporate bond markets as a catalyst for the financial sector and economic recovery in Mongolia. Building on the ongoing IMF-supported Extended Fund Facility program, the study analyzes the current status, challenges, and future development path for corporate bond markets in Mongolia. It also examines the feasibility of establishing a viable corporate bond market, exploring key obstacles and required support mechanisms, including identifying factors hindering corporate bond issuance, assessing regulatory and technical assistance needs, addressing legal and institutional roadblocks, and proposing solutions for overcoming shortfalls in market infrastructure and investor confidence. The research draws on comprehensive assessments of the financial sector, macroeconomics, and policy. Findings target critical stakeholders, including the Financial Regulatory Commission and the Mongolian Stock Exchange, to inform policies and strategies for unlocking Mongolia's potential through a vibrant, inclusive corporate bond market.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the intricate dynamics of economic growth and development in two diverse Indian states: Maharashtra and Jharkhand. With a particular emphasis on responsible consumption and production practices, we delve into the unique challenges and opportunities faced by these regions in their pursuit of sustainable development. By examining key economic indicators, policy frameworks, and innovative initiatives, we aim to provide a comprehensive analysis of the progress made towards achieving Sustainable Development Goal 12 in these contrasting economic landscapes.

title: Valuing Employment: Transaction Benefit Economics and the Future of Work Law

detail.title: Valuing Employment: Transaction Benefit Economics and the Future of Work Law
detail.abstract:
In debates about the future of work, scholars and policymakers often treat economic efficiency and distributive justice as the principal values at stake. Those who argue for the end of the employment relationship appeal to economic efficiency. They extend law and economics scholar Ronald Coase’s classic theorization of “transaction costs,” arguing that technological innovation has dramatically reduced the transaction costs of economic coordination. As a result, they argue, work today can be more efficiently performed through independent contracting and automation than through the institution of employment. In response, those who defend the legal form of employment invoke distributive justice and equality. They argue that employers should not be able to circumvent the social safety net constructed around employment simply by reorganizing production. Yet, in emphasizing the benefits of that social safety net, rather than benefits inherent to employment as a form of economic production, some concede the potential acceptability of a world without employment—so long as the social safety net lives on independently of it, whether through universal basic income, portable benefits, or other policy innovations.

In this Article, I argue that neither a transaction cost-centric analysis of employment nor one focused only on distributive justice or equality fully conceptualizes all that is at stake in the institutional design and legal regulation of how we work. This is because there are transaction benefits, not just transaction costs, associated with the organization of work. While transaction cost economics has tended to treat the social activity attendant to economic transactions as inherently costly, this social activity can have benefits too. Foremost among these are relational benefits like social trust, belonging, cooperation, and social solidarity, which accrue to individuals, groups, firms, and socio-political systems via economic interaction, coordination, and co-production. And unlike distributive justice, these benefits are inexorably tied to work’s organization; there is no quick and easy substitution for them through redistributive public policy. Transaction benefits arise, or not, at the point of production, from specific organizational forms and institutional practices, and from the legal rules that structure them.

Here, I provide the first in-depth theorization of work as a site of relational transaction benefits, with a specific focus on law’s role in shaping them. In a moment of crisis-level political polarization and social mistrust, we can no longer afford the illusion that work was ever, or should ever be, solely about material production. From Adam Smith to Émile Durkheim, scholars have long insisted that how we work shapes the quality and character of our social solidarity—the extent to which we are, sociologically speaking, a society at all. The future of work will shape the future of our society, whether we plan for it or not. It would be wiser to plan for it by proactively incentivizing the kind of work that produces social connectedness, rather than isolation and fracture. Just as the law has been used to minimize transaction costs, so too can it be used to promote transaction benefits.

title: Secured By Design: Toward A Unified Framework For Data Privacy And National Security In India And The United States

detail.abstract: India and the United States have independently developed data privacy regimes and national security surveillance architectures that operate in institutional and legislative silos. This paper argues that the siloed design is not merely an administrative inconvenience — it is a structural vulnerability that simultaneously undermines individual rights and materially weakens state security capacity. Drawing on the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 — notified on November 13, 2025 and published as G.S.R. 846(E) — the paper identifies Rule 23 read with the Seventh Schedule as India's first legislative acknowledgment that privacy law and national security law must operate as a continuum. The paper situates this development alongside India's UAPA and PMLA prosecutorial framework, the US Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the CLOUD Act, and the Supreme Court's reasoning in Carpenter v. United States. Anchored in the Delhi High Court's landmark John Doe order in Niva Bupa Health Insurance Company Limited v. Telegram FZ-LLC, it proposes five principles for a unified framework treating privacy protection and national security capacity as a single policy continuum — a framework operating at the intersection of what this paper terms cross-border intelligence and surveillance law (CISL).
