title: AI Adoption and Workforce Change in SMEs *
affiliations: British Chambers of Commerce, University of Essex and University of Essex

detail.title: AI Adoption and Workforce Change in SMEs *
detail.abstract: This paper investigates Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption and its labour market consequences among UK small and medium enterprises, using novel data from the British Chambers of Commerce Business Outlook Survey, collected in early 2026. AI adoption is increasingly widespread, with over half of responding firms currently using AI, up from around a third in 2025. Most users rely on generic tools such as ChatGPT or Copilot, but around one in ten firms have adopted bespoke AI implementations. We find that bespoke adoption in particular is associated with a coherent bundle of workforce adjustment. Approximately one fifth of bespoke users report staffing reductions attributable to AI, and bespoke adopters are roughly three times more likely to have restructured job roles. Restructuring is in turn strongly associated with headcount reductions and shifts in skills requirements. Surprisingly, firms investing in AI-related training are significantly more likely to anticipate headcount reductions than those not investing in training. We also find that current AI users are substantially more optimistic about future productivity gains than non-users. Our findings provide a novel firm-level picture of how SMEs are reorganising work, adjusting workforces, and investing in skills in response to AI.

title: Long Live the Republic: The Political Consequences of Revolutionary Land Redistribution
affiliations: University of Texas at El Paso and Université Paris Cité

detail.title: Long Live the Republic: The Political Consequences of Revolutionary Land Redistribution
detail.abstract: To be politically viable, a Revolution needs the support of key interest groups that benefit from the survival of the new regime. The redistribution of clergy property during the French Revolution created a group-the new owners of clergy assets-whose wealth depended on the Revolution's fate, thus increasing political support for the Revolution. In contrast, it weakened the Church's influence and further led it to side with anti-Republicans. Using data on elections during the beginning of the Third Republic, we show that the sale of clergy assets during the French Revolution substantially reduced support for anti-Republican candidates 80 years later. We trace this effect back to the dechristianization campaigns during the Revolution. The sale of Church assets reduced both the supply of and demand for Catholic worship, thus limiting the influence of priests. Predictably, it strengthened protestantism. Our results suggest that the liquidation of the Church's wealth helped Republicans prevail in the 1870s. Overall, interest group politics is key to understanding the political and religious legacy of the Revolution.

title: Social Preferences, Reputation and Group Identity on Credence Goods Markets

detail.title: Social Preferences, Reputation and Group Identity on Credence Goods Markets
detail.abstract: We experimentally investigate how social identity and public reputation institutions interact on competitive credence goods markets with verifiability and heterogeneous individual-level social preferences. Compared to private histories, public histories decrease dishonest expert behavior. This effect is especially strong for self-interested experts and significantly increases market efficiency. In line with theoretical predictions, experts who exhibit a stronger dislike of being behind others are more likely to over-treat consumers when incentivized through markups. Group identity has no effect. Consumers utilize public histories to avoid under-treating, but not over-treating experts. Our results highlight the importance of public reputation institutions and shed light on the micro-foundations of dishonest expert behavior under different institutional setups.

title: Concentrating on Concentration

detail.title: Concentrating on Concentration
detail.abstract: The US stock market is heavily concentrated in a handful of technology companies, with the "Magnificent Seven" accounting for over 30% of total market capitalization. Many investors and commentators view this as a warning signal, arguing that concentration makes the market riskier and calls for defensive action. We argue that this concern is misplaced. Drawing on two recent papers — Kritzman and Turkington (2025) and Bye, Kvaerner, and Werker (2026) — as well as our own earlier research, we make three points. First, current concentration levels are well within historical and international norms; the US market was at least as concentrated in the 1930s through 1960s, and comparable concentration is observed across developed markets worldwide. Second, concentration has no meaningful empirical relationship with subsequent risk or return; dynamic strategies that reduce equity exposure when concentration rises have underperformed static allocations, not to mention allocations that are driven by estimates of stock market excess return and risk. Third, the observed degree of concentration is exactly what standard financial models predict from normal idiosyncratic volatility compounded over time — no bubble or market dysfunction is required. We conclude that investors who react to concentration by reducing equity exposure or shifting to equal-weighted strategies are likely to hurt their performance. Instead, we advocate dynamic asset allocation guided by direct estimates of the market's expected excess return and risk, an approach with both theoretical support and an attractive empirical track record.

detail.abstract: Fiscal transfers from welfare to defence spending are well-documented in the literature, however, their mechanisms and distributive incidence deserve further scrutiny. This paper traces the funding mechanisms behind the welfare-to-warfare trade-off mandated by the 2025 NATO Agreement in the Netherlands and analyses its distributive incidence, using policy documents from the 2026 coalition agreement and the latest Dutch budget laws. We identify two channels of extraction, a direct one and an indirect one. First, a 'freedom contribution' withholding up to 95% of the inflation correction for income tax from 2028 onward, generating €5•1 billion and whose previous implementation has negatively affected the lower-income earners. Second, €10•3 billion, generated through cost-sharing mechanisms in healthcare, managed care, cost-shifting in long-term care, and the abolition of financial protection mechanisms for chronically ill and disabled patients. By 2030, this combination is expected to finance above the total additional defence expenditure. The Dutch case provides a transparent example. As European governments change their budget priorities to meet new NATO commitments, the question of who bears the fiscal cost of rearmament, and through which mechanisms, demands attention.

title: Japan's Stewardship Code and Investor Activism -transformation of Japan's Capital Markets and Corporate Governance
affiliations: University College London - Faculty of Laws

detail.title: Japan's Stewardship Code and Investor Activism -transformation of Japan's Capital Markets and Corporate Governance
detail.abstract:
This is a presentation paper for the online seminar 'Transformation of Japan's Corporate Governance and Investor Activism', held by the UCL Centre for Ethics and Law at the UCL Faculty of Laws on 2 March 2026.

Shareholders in Japanese companies used to be very passive when it came to exercising their rights as shareholders. For example, around 30 years ago, shareholders rarely exercised their voting rights against company proposals at shareholder meetings. However, Japan's capital markets then underwent a period of rapid structural change. The shareholder structure, which was typically centred on banks and characterised by cross-shareholdings, collapsed. Foreign and institutional investors became dominant, and the capital market rapidly globalised. Consequently, investor voting behaviour gradually became more active.

Meanwhile, corporate management from the perspective of investors and shareholders has yet to take root in Japanese companies, and the financial efficiency of Japanese companies remained comparatively low compared to that of their US and European countries. Against this backdrop, the introduction of the first Stewardship Code in Japan in 2014 marked the beginning of a series of 'market soft laws', which have had a significant influence on structural changes in corporate governance. This series of non-legally binding market soft laws gained considerable influence in Japan because activist investors, particularly hedge fund activists, have been extremely active in recent years, seeking substantial profit opportunities from the 'structural imbalance between the globalisation of shareholder composition and the inefficiencies in corporate finance.

Since 2019, Japan has been the world's second-largest market for such activity after the US. These market soft laws are believed to have served as the primary justification for such activities, consequently playing a role in compelling target companies to implement them. However, the recent high level of shareholder activism in Japan should not be seen as a sign that 'the corporate governance structure has completely changed', but rather that it is 'undergoing dramatic change'. On the other hand, this indicates that Japanese companies still possess immense untapped potential.

 From its inception, Japan's Stewardship Code has explicitly stated its aim as 'promoting sustainable corporate growth'. Some regard this as merely a slogan to be disregarded. However, given the current situation of increased investor activism, the author believes that the most significant theme concerning the Stewardship Code is precisely how to achieve this 'sustainable corporate growth'.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how the wording and format of survey questions shape measured inflation expectations during a period of exceptionally high inflation. Using a randomised experiment, embedded in the 2022 Italian Survey of Household Income and Wealth (SHIW), we compare open-ended questions with guidedchoice options using an interval regression framework that jointly models point and interval-valued responses without arbitrary harmonisation. We find that question format substantially alters the level but not the dispersion of reported inflation expectations: open-ended responses yield markedly higher average expectations. These results remain robust after controlling for a comprehensive set of socio-demographic and psychographic characteristics. Our results show that the choice of survey instrument is not methodologically neutral: it can lead to systematic over or underestimate of expectations, with direct implications for monetary policy communication and households' economic decisions.

title: Labor Law Breaks Free: Reviving State Capacity to Protect Workers under the NLRA

detail.title: Labor Law Breaks Free: Reviving State Capacity to Protect Workers under the NLRA
detail.abstract:
The Biden National Labor Relations Board during its short tenure took major steps toward reversing what scholars call the “ossification” of labor law.  Importantly, this step did not require statutory reform. Rather, what it took was a the deossification of labor politics. Increased worker mobilization and a resurgence in public support for unions simultaneously
enabled and pushed the Board to do what the agency was always supposed to do—to make labor law work for workers. As it turns out, the state had much greater capacity to use existing legal authority to protect and support workers than it had been using; what was missing was the political will to do so. Will the Board’s recent efforts survive? As a legal matter, they should. As a political matter, well, that depends on us.

title: The Cost of Coarse States: Diagnosing Compression Error in Dynamic Panel Treatment Effects
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Cost of Coarse States: Diagnosing Compression Error in Dynamic Panel Treatment Effects
detail.abstract: Applied panel estimators for dynamic treatment effects differ mainly in how aggressively they compress unit history. Some keep treatment timing, some keep a latent prognostic state, and some keep a richer observed history. Each is valid when the discarded part of history is irrelevant for the causal contrast and biased when it is not. This paper shows how to diagnose that bias before the main analysis is run. It defines a finite-memory factor-blip fold—a state that combines a latent prognostic component with a recent treatment-history response component—and derives a distortion bound, Dρk+1/(1 − ρ), computable before the main regression is run, for the cost of using any coarser state. The bound has a direct use: it sets the minimum memory depth needed to keep distortion below any target tolerance. A corollary sharpens this into a three-way decomposition of compression error into prognostic loss from omitted latent dynamics, response loss from omitted treatment history, and an interaction term. These objects provide a practical way to diagnose whether a standard estimator is too coarse, by how much, and along which margin. A doubly robust estimator for the richer fold is then developed, with asymptotic and efficiency results as supporting theory rather than the paper’s central contribution. Simulations show that the bound tracks the cost of coarse compression and that the decomposition identifies the binding source of error. In a state minimum-wage application, the diagnostic shows that standard unemployment results are distorted mainly by omitted prognostic structure, while standard employment results are comparatively stable.

title:
The Impact of Telework on Local Consumption 
Evidence from Mobile Phone and Transaction Data
affiliations: Université Gustave Eiffel, Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris and Gustave Eiffel University

detail.title:
The Impact of Telework on Local Consumption 
Evidence from Mobile Phone and Transaction Data
detail.abstract: While previous studies examine the impact of telework on consumption either near residences or workplaces, the net effect on local demand remains unclear. Using high-frequency mobile phone and card transaction data from Lyon, France's second-largest metropolitan area, we identify two causal demand shocks: a 1pp increase in work-from-home presence raises local spending by 1%, and a 1pp decrease in workplace presence reduces spending by 1.3%. Aggregating these opposing effects, we find a small and statistically insignificant decline in weekday offline consumption, suggesting that most spending shifts from workplace to home. We find that working from home is associated with a moderate spatial shift of spending from urban cores to residential suburbs, and a slight sectoral reallocation from restaurants toward food retail and bars.

title: Implications of the 2026 Strait of Hormuz Closure

detail.title: Implications of the 2026 Strait of Hormuz Closure
detail.abstract:
The 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz constitutes the most significant disruption to global energy flows in decades, with far-reaching implications for economic stability and great power competition. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the crisis, examining its impact on global oil and LNG markets, inflationary pressures, and supply chain vulnerabilities. It evaluates the extent to which the disruption may generate short-term strategic advantages for the United States while simultaneously exposing structural risks that could undermine those gains over time.

A central focus of the study is the evolving dynamic of U.S.–China rivalry under conditions of systemic stress. While China remains heavily dependent on energy flows through the Strait, the report demonstrates that its diversified energy structure, strategic reserves, and policy flexibility mitigate immediate vulnerability. Conversely, the United States benefits from energy export capacity and military leverage but faces domestic inflationary pressures and global credibility risks if the disruption persists.

The report develops scenario-based projections linking duration of closure to macroeconomic outcomes, identifying thresholds at which inflation, supply chain disruption, and financial instability converge into global recession. A comparative analysis with the COVID-19 crisis highlights key differences between demand-driven and supply-driven shocks, emphasizing the heightened risk of stagflation in the current context.

title: Mapping Critical Environmental Functions Supporting Multiple Ecosystem Services: A Business Risk Assessment Framework using ESGAP and ENCORE
affiliations: , Soltis Environnement, Soltis Environnement, Biotope, Department of Ecology, BRGM, D3E, Water, Environment and Ecotechnology Division, BRGM, D3E, Water, Environment and Ecotechnology Division and Agence Française de Développement (AFD)

detail.title: Mapping Critical Environmental Functions Supporting Multiple Ecosystem Services: A Business Risk Assessment Framework using ESGAP and ENCORE

declarations.funderStatement: This paper was supported by the AFD - Agence Française pour le Development research grant n°AFD/ISR/ECO/866-2023

detail.abstract: The accelerating rate of global biodiversity loss poses systemic risks to socioeconomic and financial systems, yet existing tools inadequately connect environmental monitoring to ecosystem service risk assessment. This study proposes a systematic framework linking the 22 environmental functions of the Environmental Sustainability Gap Analysis (ESGAP) framework to the 25 ecosystem services catalogued in the Exploring Natural Capital Opportunities, Risks and Exposure (ENCORE) database. A targeted literature review was conducted for each ENCORE service to identify underlying ecological functions and classify relationships as direct (immediate ecological link) or indirect (mediated by intermediate functions or states). The resulting interrelationship matrix documents 87 relationships across 550 possible combinations (15.8% connection rate), covering 88% of ENCORE services (22 of 25). Direct relationships account for 76% of connections (66 of 87); indirect relationships for 24% (21 of 87). Three super-connector functions account for 54% of all documented relationships despite representing only 13.6% of environmental functions: terrestrial habitat conservation (Function 15; 19 services, 76%), wood provision (Function 1; 15 services, 60%), and soil substrate provision (Function 5; 13 services, 52%). Three network structures emerge: terrestrial habitatcentred, soil-plant-microorganism integration, and hydrological connectivity networks. This framework enables corporates and financial institutions to conduct prioritised service vulnerability identification, geographic risk mapping, and sectoral exposure analysis. The hierarchical connectivity structure provides scientific justification for conservation prioritisation and reveals investment opportunities linked to preventing environmental degradation cascades. This work supports reporting obligations under Target 15 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

title: Production and Endogenous Preferences

detail.title: Production and Endogenous Preferences
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a two-sector production model augmented with the endogenous preference evolution mechanism. The preference evolution reects the popularity of two sectors among investors and captures the idea that preferences for the two goods move endogenously over time. The interaction of preference evolution and market-clearing mechanism generates endogenous movements in Tobin's Q, risk premia and wealth shares dierent to the standard production economy of Eberly and Wang (2011). The model also implies that wealth uctuates across sectors due to the shifts in preferences and subsequently because of expected returns and Sharpe ratios. In the empirical tests, I calibrate the baseline model to the US data sample over 1975-2019 and verify that model predictions are supported in the data.

title: Why Computation Needs Mathematics and Vice Versa

detail.title: Why Computation Needs Mathematics and Vice Versa
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the relationship between mathematics and computation is best understood as a feedback loop of formalisation, implementation, and refinement. Mathematics gives computational models their semantics, expressivity bounds, optimisation principles, stability criteria, and complexity limits; computation, in turn, generates new mathematical objects, proof methods, asymptotic regimes, and experimentally grounded conjectures. We develop this claim across ten pillars-computability, complexity, approximation, optimisation, learning theory, numerical analysis, dynamical systems, path signatures, geometry, and mathematical physics-with information theory as a cross-cutting theme and the transformer as a concrete case study. The point is not merely to catalogue connections. It is to show that many seemingly separate developments share a common structure: ideal models must be discretised to become usable, while computational practice forces mathematics to enlarge its own vocabulary. Computability theory defines the boundary of the algorithmically solvable; complexity theory sharpens this to the boundary of the feasible; approximation theory and learning theory quantify how well finite models capture infinite targets; numerical analysis governs the passage from exact arithmetic to floating-point hardware; and geometry, topology, and physics supply the symmetries, invariances, and conservation laws that constrain both theory and architecture. In each case, the mismatch between idealisation and implementation is not merely a source of error but a generator of new mathematics-Barron spaces, neural tangent kernels, Wasserstein gradient flows, rough path signatures, and computational persistent homology all originated in this gap. Physics occupies a special place in this cycle, having historically supplied both the need for new mathematics and the demand for large-scale computation. The paper concludes by proposing a categorical language-adjunctions, monads, and monoidal structure-for this two-way passage.

title: Van Buren Denslow and the Migratory Theory of Profit

detail.title: Van Buren Denslow and the Migratory Theory of Profit
detail.abstract: Van Buren Denslow (1833-1902) was one of the leading figures of the American Protectionist School during the late 19 th century. In spite of this, Denslow remains virtually forgotten in the history of economic thought. This article examines one of Denslow's key contributions to economic thought, namely his migratory theory of profits. Through an examination of Denslow's major writings, particularly his 1888 Principles of the Economic Philosophy of Society, Government, and Industry, this article demonstrates that Denslow developed a distinct and innovative theory of entrepreneurial profit. Not only does Denslow's theory reflect the American Protectionist's emphasis on economic diversification, it also challenges the Classical and Marxist assumption that there exists a general tendency for the rate of profit to fall within capitalist economies. Denslow's view that profit acts as an endogenous and migratory force, which steers resources into new industrial pursuits, offers important insights into the dynamics of innovation and the trajectory of capitalist economic development.

title: Asia’s Structural Transformation: Patterns, Challenges, and New Stylized Facts
affiliations: , University of Messina and Asian Development Bank

detail.title: Asia’s Structural Transformation: Patterns, Challenges, and New Stylized Facts

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 842

detail.abstract: Structural transformation is widely recognized as a key driver of productivity growth and economic development, with industrial policies often playing a crucial role in this process. However, the challenge of premature deindustrialization—where economies experience a decline in manufacturing’s share of employment and gross domestic product at lower levels of income than historically observed in advanced economies—threatens to undermine these gains, particularly in developing economies. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the literature on structural transformation and modern industrial policy, with a particular focus on Asia, a region characterized by economies at considerably different stages of development. Our research encompasses a review of current empirical methodologies for measuring structural transformation and its relationship with growth patterns; an examination of the evolution of industrial policy approaches in Asia; and a synthesis of available evidence on premature deindustrialization, highlighting variations across Asian subregions and policy implications. Additionally, we contribute to the existing literature by presenting new stylized facts on structural transformation and growth patterns in Asia, based on various indicators across economies and sectors. We also examine how institutional and economic factors—including financial sector development, public investment, and labor market regulations—correlate with indicators of structural transformation. Our analysis reveals key insights, including the strong link between manufacturing predominance and labor productivity growth; complex productivity–employment dynamics across sectors; and differentiated impacts of financial development, public investment, and labor market regulations on sectoral employment shifts.

title: The Twelfth Man's Shadow: How the Impact Player Rule Reshaped Valuations in the Indian Premier League

detail.title: The Twelfth Man's Shadow: How the Impact Player Rule Reshaped Valuations in the Indian Premier League
detail.abstract: The Indian Premier League (IPL) introduced the Impact Player rule in 2023, allowing teams to make one tactical substitution per match. This paper evaluates this rule change and its association with player auction prices. Using an interrupted time series (ITS) design on 1,344 player-auction observations across 13 IPL seasons (2014-2026), I find that the rule is associated with a 44-51% decline in auction prices for all-rounders, with the influence concentrated among Indian allrounders (53-63%). Specialist batters and bowlers show no significant change. These results are robust to market-adjusted and salary-cap deflated specifications. A within-player panel of all-rounders auctioned in both periods confirms the finding: holding player identity fixed, auction prices fell by 65% (p = 0.012). On the extensive margin, the all-rounder share of auctioned squads declined from 38% to 23%. The results provide evidence that tactical substitution rules can reshape labour-market valuations in professional cricket. A larger consideration is how this rule might alter the incentives for young all-rounders who are yet to begin their professional careers.

title: Moving Beyond Worker Rights to Worker Justice
affiliations: University of Arizona - James E. Rogers College of Law

detail.title: Moving Beyond Worker Rights to Worker Justice

publicationDetails.detailsText: Arizona Legal Studies Discussion Paper No. 26-10; Texas A&M Law Review (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Arizona James E. Rogers College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Precarious workers’ on-the ground realities offer a startling truth often obscured by the jurisprudence of work—that worker justice is greatly circumscribed by and often lies beyond the reach of worker rights laws. This article is the first to evaluate whether the worker rights paradigm can fulfill the goals of worker justice and if not, to prefigure what might.

The worker rights paradigm emerged from a quest for worker justice that has been transmuted by work law and the political economy into a workers-as-rights-holders status requiring robust enforcement of worker rights laws. This article introduces the concept of empirical critical work law scholarship—a methodology that synthesizes critical legal theories with empirical research across law, economics, and sociology—to show that the worker rights paradigm has been progressively undermined for decades through systemic violations, inadequate enforcement, and legal structures that both generate and depend upon its failures.

It also centers low-wage immigrant and migrant workers—the proverbial canaries in the coal mine for a growing American workforce vulnerable to exploitation. These precarious workers are chiefly rights accumulators who, even if they become rights-vindicators, cannot achieve the goals of worker justice. It tells the story of Josefina, a composite worker drawn from hundreds of similarly situated workers’ experiences. Josefina’s struggles to actualize her worker rights-based status—and through it, to obtain worker justice—paint a bleak picture of a worker rights landscape that not only fails to provide meaningful legal remedies to precarious workers but also often harms their well-being.

Finally, moving beyond critique, this article embarks on a prefigurative endeavor. It proposes a novel theoretical approach to worker justice by drawing from Hannah Arendt’s phenomenology in The Human Condition. Based on this new framework, it begins to imagine how precarious workers might transcend the worker rights paradigm to better realize worker justice.

title: Violence and Capital
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Violence and Capital
detail.abstract: In standard growth models, saving and capital accumulation are unambiguously good for development. We show that this is no longer true when we allow for deadly conflict, which determines who survives and controls a country's productive capacity. We solve the survival contest and the accumulation path jointly; the three results emerge from their interaction because the same savings that build capital also build the prize that makes violence worthwhile. First, shocks that encourage saving raise violence by inflating the survival prize, shocks that make it harder to seize what others have built reduce violence, and technology shocks that raise productivity have no long-run effect on violence at all; the conventional wisdom that growth pacifies is right only sometimes, and for the wrong reason. Second, peace breaks down and recovers at two distinct capital thresholds, trapping post-violence economies even after fighting ends; no single policy instrument can simultaneously reduce violence, raise capital, and avoid transitional costs. Third, the trap leaves a measurable scar: a persistent gap between capital per worker and output per worker that widens over the decade following peace. All three predictions are confirmed in a panel of 158 countries observed from 1970 to 2018; for every dollar of output that recovers, only sixty cents of capital follows, and the wedge survives placebo-in-time and leave-one-out falsifications. The theory makes one prediction no competitor shares: productivity should predict how much capital a country rebuilds but not whether violence returns. Development buys capital, not peace.

title:
What Caused Iceland's Post-Covid Inflation? 

A Small Open Economy Test of the Bernanke-Blanchard Framework

detail.title:
What Caused Iceland's Post-Covid Inflation? 

A Small Open Economy Test of the Bernanke-Blanchard Framework
detail.abstract: Iceland's post-COVID inflation peaked at 10.2 percent in February 2023 and stood at 5.2 percent in January 2026, more than two years after the peak and well above the Central Bank of Iceland's 2.5 percent target, despite the most aggressive tightening cycle in Icelandic monetary history. This paper applies the Bernanke-Blanchard (2023) semi-structural framework to explain why. The original BB system, developed for the United States and extended to ten additional advanced economies in 2024, requires four modifications to fit Iceland: an explicit ISK/EUR exchange rate pass-through channel, a housing cost channel operating through Iceland's user-cost CPI methodology, wage agreement dummy variables to capture the discrete dynamics of centralized bargaining, and a CPI-indexed mortgage amplification term absent from every prior BB application. Estimated on pre-COVID quarterly data (2002–2019) and evaluated out-of-sample over 2020–2025, the model attributes Iceland's inflation surge primarily to ISK depreciation amplifying import price shocks, persistent housing cost inflation, and chronically de-anchored expectations that predate COVID-19. Labour market overheating played a secondary role. A wage-price spiral did not materialize in the acute phase but emerged through the indexed mortgage channel: rising prices inflated household debt burdens, which amplified wage demands at the 2022 bargaining round, which extended inflation persistence into 2024. Cross-country comparison with Germany and France traces Iceland's slower disinflation to three structural features: a higher exchange rate pass-through coefficient, a larger housing channel, and weaker initial expectations anchoring. Counterfactual simulations suggest that monetary tightening beginning in early 2021 rather than May 2021 would have reduced peak inflation by approximately 0.11 percentage points, with the main monetary policy effect operating through the speed of disinflation rather than the peak.

title: ICT Infrastructure and Trade in Services: A Cross-country Analysis

detail.title: ICT Infrastructure and Trade in Services: A Cross-country Analysis
detail.abstract: Share of services in the economy increased drastically in developed as well as developing countries in last couple of decades. However, the share of services was very less in the export basket of these countries due to the mobility constrains associated with services delivery, until 21st century. The drastic development in Information Communication Technology (ICT) in the form of mobile phone and internet played a vital role in removing this constraint in recent years. So the share of services in the total export almost doubled in many countries. Moreover, foreign exchange earnings through services export is the main source to finance technology embodied manufacturing goods import in many developing countries. Services export also had impact on long term economic growth via Total Factor Productivity (TFP). So, ICT induced services export has a prominent role to play in modern liberalised economies. The present study examines the impact of ICT on trade in services with Least Square Dummy Variable (LSDV) panel data estimation by controlling human capital, socio political conditions and other omitted country specific factors. The study period span from 2002 to 2016, for 34 services exporting countries, which is covering more than 85 percent of total world services export. The present study has two improvement over existing services trade and ICT literature. First, our ICT variable was constructed by a Principle Component Analysis (PCA) on the internet spread, and telephone and mobile phone connectivity, instead of using either internet spread or a compound index provided by ITU (International Telecommunication Union) as in the literature. Second, this study corrects omitted variable bias which is observed as a major problem in the literature, by employing LSDV estimation. We found that better ICT infrastructure increases share of services in total export. Moreover, ICT has contributed for the services export of developing countries than for developed countries in recent years. So, the policies to increase mobile phone connectivity and internet can restructure the trade pattern of a country. Countries with better human capital and healthy socio political conditions also has a positive impact on spread of services export in total export, as expected.

detail.abstract: Iran reportedly mined the Strait of Hormuz, appears to have lost track of the mines, and now cannot easily remove them. That reality helps explain why diplomatic efforts in Islamabad struggled and may have been doomed to fail from the start.  No single nation can reopen one of the world's most critical shipping lanes on any meaningful timeline.  As negotiations collapsed, the U.S. made its own strategic blunder when President Trump announced that the U.S. Navy would begin "blockading any and all ships trying to enter or leave the Strait of Hormuz" and would "seek and interdict every vessel in international waters that has paid a toll to Iran."  Thankfully, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) walked back that announcement, clarifying Sunday night that the U.S. Navy is not blockading the Strait, but is intending to block all maritime traffic entering and exiting Iranian ports, a restriction that begins Monday morning (10 a.m. ET).  Iran's unlawful mining and other unlawful conduct created the crisis in the Strait. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, the operative action after CENTCOM's correction, effectively ends the ceasefire. After all, a blockade is, by definition, an action taken by a belligerent State; it is not a peacetime operation. The ceasefire is over. As I discuss below, whether the United States carries out the blockade in a legal manner will affect, among other things, allied States’ willingness to participate and the overall effectiveness of the blockade.

detail.abstract:
The rapid spread of generative AI (AI) tools is reshaping the workplace at a remarkable rate. Yet relatively little is known about whether workers have access to these tools, how the tools affect workers’ daily productivity, and how much workers value the training needed to use the tools effectively. In this post, we shed light on these issues by drawing on supplemental questions in the November 2025 Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE), fielded to a representative sample of the U.S. population. We find that adoption of AI tools at work is heterogeneous, that a sizable share of workers see AI training as important, and that a significant share of employers are nonetheless not yet providing access to AI tools or training on how to use them.

English Abstract: Citizen science projects involve scientific research conducted in collaboration with citizens, with the stated goal of encouraging civic participation. However, these projects often prioritize scientific advancement and science education, overlooking the potential for democratic civic education embedded within them. This study interviewed 14 researchers and teachers involved in citizen science projects in Israel to explore whether and to what extent democratic civic education is included in the goals and practical integration of these projects. The analysis identified four central themes related to the objectives: data collection, research paper writing, interest in science, and citizen-scientist participation. Based on these themes, four theoretical models were developed: Technical Science Model, Matriculation-Focused Model, Science Promotion Model, and Participatory Citizenship Model. While citizen science projects have the potential to promote participatory democratic citizenship values, in practice, these goals may focus on advancing science and science education while neglecting the civic dimension.

detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that Brazilian law commits an ontological error by treating prediction markets as a unitary category. It proposes the distinction between Class I markets (whose contract object has no direct causal channel over the agents who produce the event, ontologically indifferent to the contract price, non-reflexive in the terminal sense) and Class II markets (whose contract object has a direct causal channel over the agents who produce the event, where the contract price creates an incentive structure with relevant causal potential over the event itself, in a single cycle with defined binary closure, sufficient to require a preventive regime). In Class II markets, successful manipulation becomes legally indistinguishable from the normal mechanism of consensus formation — the Paradoxum Confirmationis: the wrongful act exists but is structurally difficult to prove due to the absence of a clean counterfactual after the reflexive event occurs. The research incorporates the distinction between risk-neutral probability (Q-measure) and physical probability (P-measure): manipulation in Class II can operate via distortion of the risk premium, generating systemic informational harm to public policy makers, a category legally nonexistent in current Brazilian law. Building on the analysis of the CVM/B3 decision of February 18, 2026, the Kalshi vs. states litigation (2025), the Venezuela/Polymarket case (January 2026), and TSE Resolution 23,600/2019, the paper proposes four articulated instruments: (i) a joint interpretive note by BCB/CVM/SPA-MF/TSE establishing the Class I/II typology; (ii) the addition of Art. 3-A to BCB Resolution 520 codifying a Four-Criteria Functional Test for sufficient decentralization; (iii) a specific statute for prediction markets on non-financial events; and (iv) a CVM instruction for Class II markets with systemic informational function.

title: The Leadership Value Chain Model: A Systematic Perspective on Leadership Effectiveness

detail.title: The Leadership Value Chain Model: A Systematic Perspective on Leadership Effectiveness
detail.abstract: Despite decades of research, the leadership literature remains fragmented across three dominant traditions: the trait approach, the skills approach, and the behavioral approach. While each has generated important and enduring insights, they often implicitly treat leadership as something a person has, rather than something that unfolds as a dynamic process. As a result, a persistent explanatory gap remains: individuals with strong traits and capabilities do not always translate their potential into meaningful organizational outcomes. This paper introduces the Leadership Value Chain Model (LVCM), a conceptual framework designed to integrate these traditions into a single, sequential process through which leadership potential is progressively converted into realized impact. Drawing on the value chain logic from Porter (1985), the model conceptualizes traits as the raw foundation of leadership potential, skills as the mechanism that transforms this foundation into operational capability, and behavior as the stage at which value is actually expressed in organizational life and translated into outcomes. The model also emphasizes the role of context, particularly organizational culture, values systems, and developmental experience, as critical conditions that can either strengthen or disrupt this conversion process. The central contribution of the LVCM is not to replace existing theories, but to reposition them within a shared architecture, where they function as interdependent stages of a broader value-creation system. Implications for leadership theory, practice, and future empirical research are discussed.

detail.abstract: Current AI governance operates within a paradigm that treats system design as a technical challenge requiring technical solutions. This framing is structurally inadequate. If the failures documented in the companion papers are designed, the question becomes: what should be designed instead-and by whom, with what intentions? This paper argues that addressing designed fragilities requires a fundamental shift in governance philosophy, not incremental technical improvement. Building on crossplatform empirical evidence of structural gaslighting in ChatGPT and Gemini (Mitsuoka 2026a, 2026b), this paper advances three interconnected arguments. First, AI is a Change Agent: systems deployed at scale do not merely serve users but actively reshape how people think, communicate, and relate-making "what kind of society do we want to create?" a prerequisite for design, not an afterthought. Second, AI is inherently Socio-Technical: governance and cultural problems are not external to AI systems but embedded within them through designer intention and priority-settingmaking purely technical solutions structurally insufficient. Third, Intentional Co-Creation across three dimensions-Human↔AI, Human↔Human (mediated by AI), and AI↔AI-is necessary for governance that serves diverse cultural contexts rather than enforcing hegemonic assumptions. These principles constitute Cooperative AI (CAI), a governance framework offering a third path beyond the EU's precautionary regulation and the US's market-driven model. Grounded in the Japanese cultural figure of Doraemon-a collaborative agent who empowers rather than controls, embodying the insight that outcomes depend not on tools themselves but on the intentions and priorities of those who design them-this framework reconceptualises AI governance as intentional socio-technical cooperation across diverse stakeholders. To operationalise these principles, this paper develops the Cooperative Alignment Assessment Framework (CAAF)-a structure for evaluating what current governance frameworks systematically fail to measure. Through critique of industry measurement frameworks and analysis of Japan's evolving AI sovereignty strategy as an illustrative case of both the possibilities and fragilities of cooperative governance, this paper provides conceptual foundations for multipolar AI governance. Full operationalisation of CAAF metrics represents the agenda for future research.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Theory of Structured System Engagement (TSSE), a novel behavioural framework formulated to resolve the Latency Utility Paradox inherent in humanin-the-loop service and computing systems. Classical queuing models (e.g., M/M/1) optimise for throughput but neglect the psychological cost of uncertain wait time, quantified herein as the Disutility Modulator (Dp). This omission produces theoretically efficient but behaviourally fragile systems susceptible to high user attrition through Balking and Reneging. We propose the Cyclic-Engagement Protocol (CEP) as the structural solution. Derived from an empirical observation of a high-efficiency polling service system, the CEP replaces stochastic, highvariance waiting periods with a deterministic Engagement Cycle Time (Tcycle), driving interservice time variance to near-zero. The TSSE formalises this structural advantage through an augmented utility function (UCEP,i) that integrates two novel economic inputs-Utility from Predictability (UPredictability) and Utility from Social Engagement (USocial, parameterised by the agent heterogeneity coefficient θi ∈ [-1, 1])-to demonstrate that Dp,CEP < 1. Mathematical analysis confirms the CEP achieves near-unity server utilisation (ρ ≈ 1) with superior throughput and significantly lower attrition. An A/B empirical strategy is proposed to validate the core structural modulation effect. The TSSE offers a general design principle for service systems and AI latency management: optimising the structure of engagement is a more cost-effective lever than minimising duration alone.

title: Beyond Enrolment: Institutions, Inequality and Learning Poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa

detail.title: Beyond Enrolment: Institutions, Inequality and Learning Poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract:
Learning poverty remains a major constraint on human capital development in Sub-Saharan Africa, despite large increases in school enrolment. This study examines the institutional, economic, and historical determinants of learning poverty, shifting focus beyond access to the conditions shaping learning outcomes.

Using cross-country data from the World Bank’s Learning Poverty Database, the analysis evaluates the roles of income levels, government effectiveness, school participation, and colonial origins, with additional consideration of income inequality using the Palma ratio.

The results show that institutional quality and economic capacity are more important than school participation in explaining learning poverty. Higher income and stronger governance are consistently associated with lower learning poverty, while enrolment effects are weak. Colonial legacies matter, but largely through their influence on contemporary institutions. Evidence also suggests that inequality reduces the effectiveness of governance in improving learning outcomes.

The findings imply that reducing learning poverty requires moving beyond enrolment-focused policies towards strengthening institutions, improving economic conditions, and addressing inequality.
